As written, a developer cannot implement any of these. Real, and worth fixing.

COLLISION 3 — WRONG, and the proposed fix would damage the spec. It rests on the false premise that every `sys_audit_log` row comes from a trigger. DB-04's own action list includes `login`, `print` and `export` — none of which is a row change on an audited business table, so none can be trigger-produced. DB-04 also withholds only "UPDATE or DELETE permission for the application login" from `sys_audit_log`, i.e. the application does hold INSERT (NFR-105 at line 245 says the same). So `delete-attempt` is straightforwardly an application-written row when the app refuses a deletion — exactly the pattern AC-09 (line 838) and WF-62 already use ("refused ... and the refusal is logged"). Separately, AC-28 is not about DELETE at all: its When is "attempts to **change** it", an UPDATE, which DB-07 (line 549) says is blocked by a trigger that does fire. Deleting `delete-attempt` from DB-04 would remove a genuine security-relevant audit event.

COLLISION 1 — NOT A CONTRADICTION, at most an unstated detail. Section_3:1493 states the design intent outright — "the file fingerprint check that catches a genuine code pasted onto a doctored document." There is no PAdES verification of the recipient's file anywhere, so "a PAdES signature over that content must fail" describes a check the system does not perform. AC-25 is a correct, precise instance of M9-18.

(2) AC-01 label content vs label timing — STANDS, and is real, but the reviewer misassigns the error. AC-01 is NOT the wrong party: its own When column has the clerk "accepts the sample after the condition checklist, and prints the label", which matches section_3:400 M3-20 [MUST] — "A barcode label is printed for each physical item at the moment of acceptance, not at registration. M3-23 [MUST] (section_3:408) reinforces this: "The turnaround clock starts at the moment of sample acceptance (not request date, not receipt)", and M3-24 computes the due date from that acceptance clock start. Allocations and due dates exist only from Accepted (WF-38, §9.1 Accepted row "Computes each allocation's due date", §9.2 Pending row). AC-02 tests one atomic batch action, and WF-97 (number allotted at commit, inside the same transaction) plus WF-98 (locked counter row) guarantee 30 consecutive numbers for a committed batch of 30. The reviewer's own replacement wording is self-refuting: it deletes "with no gaps" and substitutes "consecutive within this batch", which is the same requirement in different words. confirmed.location: section_5_nfr_plan.md ARC-13 (line 331), ARC-13 stack table PDF and signing rows (lines 340-341), ARC-17 (line 354), DB-04 (line 546), NFR-103 (line 241), NFR-70 (line 165), OPEN-Q-T7 (line 919)

confirmed.problem: The three riskiest decisions in this document are all unresolved or wrong for this deployment. (3) The audit trail written by database triggers with a session-variable identity (DB-04, DB-05, NFR-103) welds the application to one database engine, breaks every ORM and migration tool's assumptions, forbids the scheduled jobs the document itself requires, and — as noted separately — cannot deliver AC-42 or AC-28.

Confine the change to the PDF-generation and digital-signing rows of the §24.4 table (parts/section_5_nfr_plan.md:340-341). Do not touch ARC-13, DB-04 or NFR-103.

1. Restate the PDF row as capability-based rather than language-based: "A library, available for the language chosen under ARC-13/ARC-14, that produces tagged PDF with a real text layer (NFR-70), applies PAdES signatures with long-term validation, and renders Telugu and Devanagari correctly (NFR-93). Candidates exist on every stack recommended above — for example ReportLab with pyHanko on Python, or a mature PDF library on .NET or Java. A second runtime purely for document generation is a last resort: if one is unavoidable, it is recorded as an explicit exception in the ARC-06 configuration record with its own ARC-16 offline vendoring plan, because a district unit with no information-technology support must patch and rebuild only one dependency tree." Delete "Recommended: Apache PDFBox or iText (Java or .NET)" and the sentence beginning "If the main application is PHP or Python".

2. Add one new requirement near ARC-16: "ARC-16a — Every third-party library's licence is recorded in the technical manual and must be compatible with NFR-113's handover of the source code to Central Silk Board as its property. iText in particular is permitted only if a commercial licence is purchased in Central Silk Board's name; its default AGPL terms conflict with that handover. [MUST]"

Explicitly reject the reviewer's two other proposals: mandating ".NET 8 with ASP.NET Core" contradicts ARC-13 ("CloudZoo's own language, framework and database decide the stack"), ARC-14, and the row's own deciding reason ("Pick the one the developer is fastest in ... Anything the developer has not shipped before: reject"); and rewriting DB-04 to a repository-layer audit with triggers on five tables contradicts NFR-103, AC-30, AC-42 and research_nabl_17025.md rule A1, which states that application-layer-only auditing is not acceptable.
confirmed.verifierReason:
The quote is verbatim (parts/section_5_nfr_plan.md:340, SPEC.md:5056). But only one of the finding's three legs survives, and the proposed fix is wrong on all three.

LEG 1 (OPEN-Q-T7 blocks Phase 1) — DOES NOT STAND. The reviewer missed that this is already handled. §28.1 is titled "Must be answered before Phase 1 coding begins"; OPEN-Q-T7 already carries a "Recommended default if no answer" column reading "Assume a separate application integrating by a documented interface"; Phase 0 (2 weeks, §26.2) contains PLN-07 "Determine CloudZoo ERP's language, framework, database, whether new tables may be added, and its integration surface (ARC-13). [MUST]" and PLN-04 "Confirm the open-question list ... and record the answer or the agreed default for each. Anything still open after this session is escalated in writing." Phase 0's acceptance milestone is "a signed-off open-question register". So Phase 0 exists precisely to close this before Phase 1 coding, and a default already exists; the reviewer's "10 working days / default is binding" clause is a restatement. The sub-point that DB-02/DB-33/NFR-43 cannot be guaranteed inside CloudZoo's schema is partly answered by their own wording — all three are scoped to "the application's database login", not to all principals.

LEG 3 (trigger-written audit trail is over-engineering) — DOES NOT STAND, and the fix is actively harmful. parts/research_nabl_17025.md:275 (rule A1, derived from ISO 17025 clause 7.5.2) mandates exactly this: "Implement as an append-only history table per audited entity written by a database trigger, or event sourcing. Application-layer-only auditing is not acceptable — a direct SQL edit must still be caught." The reviewer's replacement (audit written by "a single repository layer", triggers on only five tables) is the application-layer-only design the source brief rejects, and would break NFR-103, AC-30 and AC-42 for every other audited table. The supporting claims are also overstated: triggers do not "break every ORM and migration tool" (ARC-29 requires numbered forward-only migrations, which is where triggers live), and DB-05 does not "forbid the scheduled jobs" — a job is application code and can set the session user, and there is no requirement anywhere prohibiting it. §25.6 contains 18 rules (DB-25..DB-42), about 11 trigger-based, not "35 trigger sets".

LEG 2 (the PDF/signing rows) — STANDS, narrowly. Two real defects, both confined to two table cells:
(a) The licence word appears nowhere in the document in this sense — I grepped parts/ and SPEC.md for "licen[cs]e", "AGPL", "GPL", "dual-licen", "permissive"; the only hits are about standards documents and CCA-licensed Certifying Authorities. iText is named as a recommendation with no licence caveat, while NFR-113 makes the source code "the property of Central Silk Board" and ARC-28 hands the repository over. That is a genuine, unaddressed procurement/legal exposure.
(b) "Java or .NET ... run the document component as a separate small service or command-line tool" is an inference the research does not support — research_india_commercial.md:727 says only "a PDF library that supports PDF/UA tagging", and never names a language or a side-car. Two of the three languages recommended in the row directly above (PHP 8.3/Laravel, Python/Django) would therefore be forced into a second runtime and a second dependency tree on a server the document itself describes as having "no on-site information-technology support" (line 301), in tension with ARC-06's single documented configuration and ARC-16's MUST that everything be vendored for offline rebuild. The premise is also questionable: pyHanko (PAdES/LTV, permissive) plus ReportLab give a Python stack all three capabilities without a side-car.

Severity reduced to Minor because ARC-17 already places the library behind a replaceable interface and NFR-70 already defers the final choice to a capability test before Phase 1 coding, so the wrong recommendation is cheap to correct; and because the cell is explicitly a "Recommended:" with an honest-alternatives column.

confirmed.verifierReason:
Both quotes are verbatim (SPEC.md:4281 and SPEC.md:262-263), and the omission is real: I searched "auditor", "assessor", "read-only", "read replica", "CSTRI", "CSB HQ", "headquarters", "consolidated", "SELECT only", "database login" and "sys_role", and no requirement anywhere creates either account, and neither is a column in M21.3. The Part A rows are written in operative language and, unlike "Public Verifier (anonymous, no login)", are not annotated as loginless, so Part A does promise two accounts that Part D never builds. Part D's own screen tables make this worse, not better: M21.1 lists "Permission Matrix Viewer | Administrator, Quality Manager, assessors", M20.1 lists "Register Viewer | All staff, assessors", M16 lists "Conditions Log | All staff, auditors" and M8 lists "Archive and retrieval | Any authorised role / auditor" — screens whose stated users have no role that could grant them access.

But the reviewer inflates it to Major and the fix is wrong in four concrete ways.

Severity is Minor, not Major, because (a) the substantive assessor need is already met — M20-37 gives a filterable audit-trail extract "for producing to an assessor", M21-13 prints the matrix, NFR-120 makes every register readable without the software, and M21-81's "escorts for external assessors" shows the document's operative model is escorted access; (b) M21-11 makes the matrix "data, not code", so an Auditor role is configurable at go-live without a code change, which defeats "the developer will not build it" for everything except the database-level property; (c) the HQ half is largely subsumed by M20-38/40/42/44 (return plus immutable, locked, read-only, printable snapshots), and cross-unit consolidated reporting is an explicit non-goal (N9) deferred by OPEN-Q-T28, so gap #48's "Important" rating is already dispositioned rather than ignored. The reviewer's premise that every Part A §4.1 row must be an M21.3 column is also not the document's own convention: "Technical Manager" (line 254) has no column either, and "VR Verifier" is a column but is absent from §4.1.

Fix defects: (1) ID collision — M21-14 already exists ("Every permission denial shall be logged...") and M21-15 already exists (the blinding rule); M21 runs continuously to M21-82, so the proposed IDs would duplicate two live requirements and, if renumbered, break every cross-reference through M21-82. (2) "R on every view/read/print row" for HQ directly contradicts §4.1 line 263, which forbids HQ from seeing "individual customers' identities or their individual results", and contradicts M21-80, which gates aggregate/research exports on the customer having been informed in advance; blanket R would grant HQ "Customer master — view identity" and record-level "Registers and reports — view / print". (3) "its database login holds SELECT only" plus an acceptance check performed "directly against the database login" gives an external auditor a database credential; DB-02, NFR-43, M21-31, WF-101 and M4-21 all speak of a single "application's database login" and the architecture gives no end user direct database access, so this is a new architectural element smuggled in as an acceptance check. (4) An Auditor or HQ login collides with M21-01, which requires every login to belong to a named person linked to a staff record (M13) or a portal customer contact (M18); an external NABL assessor, CAG auditor or HQ officer is neither.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part D M21-43 (approx. L4425) and Part C M8-46 (approx. L2491)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Nothing in M21-43 or M8-46 requires the certificate behind tier (c) to come from a CCA-licensed Certifying Authority, so a solo developer can satisfy the document's stated design target with a locally generated self-signed PKCS#12 key. The research is emphatic and specific about this: a self-signed certificate is not a digital signature under section 3 of the IT Act, 2000, is not one of the notified techniques under section 3A, will display "At least one signature has problems / The signer's identity is unknown" to an exporter's bank or an auditor, and "the spec should say so in exactly those words so the developer does not quietly ship it as the real thing." The spec's only warning covers a pasted signature image, which is a different failure mode. The Unit Incharge will believe every issued report carries a legally recognised signature when it may carry nothing of the kind.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The finding's central factual claim is false. It asserts that "Nothing in M21-43 or M8-46 requires the certificate behind tier (c) to come from a CCA-licensed Certifying Authority," but M8-46 (SPEC.md:2490) literally reads: "Signing supports three tiers, selected by configuration: (i) a system electronic signature ... (ii) a signature applied with a certificate issued by a licensed certifying authority; (iii) an Aadhaar-based electronic signature service." Tiers (ii) and (iii) are exactly the two things the proposed fix asks to be added, and the reviewer's own QUOTE field for its companion Major finding reproduces that clause verbatim — so it read the text and then wrote a Blocker denying it exists.

The M21-43 quote itself is accurate (SPEC.md:4424; authored source parts/section_4_functional_support.md:1499). But the substantive risk — a solo developer shipping a locally generated self-signed PKCS#12 as the customer-facing signature — is pinned down in at least four further places: (1) the glossary at SPEC.md:319 defines DSC as "A cryptographic credential issued by a licensed Indian Certifying Authority, held on a hardware token, used to sign documents with legal effect"; (2) the technology-choice row at SPEC.md:5057 specifies the signing interface as "three interchangeable implementations: a local key file (development only), a hardware security module holding an organisational Document Signer certificate, and an electronic-signature service provider" — the local key file is expressly development-only; (3) Phase 6 at SPEC.md:5419 scopes "the stronger digital signature (an organisational Document Signer certificate on a hardware security module, with trusted timestamping and long-term validation)" with the acceptance milestone "the resulting report validates as digitally signed in an ordinary PDF reader," which a self-signed certificate cannot pass; (4) ARC-27, ARC-38 and ARC-40 govern signing-key custody (OS key store, HSM, or USB token in the organisation's custody; test key with a distinct key identifier). The claim that "the spec's only warning covers a pasted signature image" is therefore also wrong.

Research-confidence check cuts against the fix as well. parts/research_india_commercial.md §4.3 (lines 416-424) marks the entire legal chain "[ASSUMPTION]", not verified, and hedges the very point the fix would state as fact: "It may still be an 'electronic signature' under Section 3A if a notified reliable technique is used, but self-signed PKCS#12 is not one of the notified techniques." The reviewer characterises this as "emphatic and specific" and would have the SRS assert flatly that a self-signed certificate "is not a digital signature under section 3 ... is not a notified electronic-signature technique under section 3A." That inverts the document's established convention of flagging unconfirmed research (cf. OPEN-Q-C7 "The research could not confirm the two-code requirement from an official source", OPEN-Q-B12), and would introduce an unverified-fact-as-fact defect — the category this same reviewer polices elsewhere in the run.

The fix is also mechanically defective. M8-46 has no "tier (c)"; its tiers are (i)/(ii)/(iii), so "Tier (c) means ..." appended there dangles and merely restates (ii) and (iii). "Any release that applies a self-signed certificate to a customer-facing report fails acceptance" contradicts SPEC.md:5057 (local key file permitted in development) and the phase plan, which deliberately defers the HSM Document Signer certificate to Phase 6 while Phases 1-5 go live on the in-application electronic signature plus the QR verification record. The fix also flattens the research's [VERIFIED] point that CCA treats a Document Signer certificate as "not a replacement for the signature of the organisation's authorised signatory," which matters for a report that must identify the authorising scientist.

Finally, the finding is duplicative: the same reviewer's separate Major finding on the M8-46 versus M21-43 tier-list mismatch already carries "a certificate from a Certifying Authority licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities" into the reconciled tier (c). That is the correct home for the only residual point here — M21-43(c) is worded loosely when read in isolation — and it is at most a Minor editorial tightening (a cross-reference from M21-43 to M8-46), not a Blocker.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part C M10-05 acceptance check (approx. L2783) versus the Part A glossary entry for "Lot" (approx. L343)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The document's own glossary states the current rule correctly: "**Lot** | The unit of raw-silk grading; under the current amended Indian Standard, two to four cartons of 30 kg each, or one to two bales of 60 kg each." That is IS 15090 Amendment No. 1 of February 2007, verified [F, S4]. M10-05's acceptance check then registers a lot of four 60-kg-class bales — twice the permitted maximum — as the worked example a staff member will run at acceptance. Worse, no requirement anywhere validates lot composition against the standard, so the system will happily accept and certify a consignment that cannot lawfully be one grading lot, and the resulting Grading Certificate is defective on its face. Twenty-five books per bale is also inconsistent with the glossary's own "twenty-two to thirty books" only at the top end, but the bale count is the substantive error.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote exists but the reviewer has misread it, mis-assigned the document type, and proposed a fix that would contradict four other places in the specification.

1. QUOTE — exists, but truncated in a load-bearing way. D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\SPEC.md L2782 reads: "A conditioning job is registered against a **lot**, which contains a stated number of **bales** (or cartons), each containing a stated number of **books**." The reviewer elided "(or cartons)". The amended rule permits "2 to 4 cartons of 30 kg each", and IS 15090's own original cl. 3.2 phrases a four-package lot as "a lot of 4 bales of 30 kg each" (D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\parts\research_silk_domain.md L245). The acceptance check states no bale mass, so the reviewer's "four 60-kg-class bales = twice the permitted maximum" is an assumption he supplied, not text the document contains. Four 30-kg packages is exactly at the permitted maximum, not double it.

2. CATEGORY ERROR — M10 does not produce a Grading Certificate. M10's opening paragraph (L2749) states the conditioned-mass document "is a **weight and settlement document**, not a quality document, and it must not be forced into the same table, the same layout, the same numbering series or the same approval path as a test report." M10-01, M10-04 and M10-29 (title: "Record and Report of Conditioned Mass of Raw Silk") keep it deliberately separate from the Grading Certificate. Amendment No. 1's rule is expressly scoped — "**The unit of grading** shall be for one lot" — so it governs grading, not how much silk may be weighed for invoice settlement. The claim that "the resulting Grading Certificate is defective on its face" is about a document M10-05 does not produce.

3. NOT A CONTRADICTION IN CONTEXT — the document's operational "lot" is the submitted consignment, and this is settled in at least five places, all with counts far above two bales: M3-03 acceptance check "Register a lot of 20 bales as one sample with 20 sub-unit rows" (L1618); M3-15 "Registering 40 bales must take one screen and one save" (L1640); M3 rule 6 "A lot of 20 bales is one sample with 20 sub-units... one result per lot for grading purposes" (L1784); L487 "A customer says 'about 20 bales'; 18 arrive"; and the M10 field table's own validation for "Number of bales in the lot" — "**One or more**" (L2851). M10-05's four-bale example is squarely consistent with all of these. Also relevant: OPEN-Q-C10 (L2822) recommends billing conditioning **per bale**, which presupposes multi-bale lots.

4. THE FIX WOULD INTRODUCE NEW CONTRADICTIONS — the proposed M10-05a is a [MUST] that refuses to proceed above two 60-kg bales and whose acceptance check is "Register five bales of 60 kg; blocked". That directly breaks M3-03's 20-bale acceptance check, M3-15's 40-bale bulk registration, M3 rule 6, and the M10 field-table validation "One or more". It would also misfire against the ISA specification set, which the document supports as a first-class alternative (M1-49 at L1363, separate ISA catalogue records at L1327, glossary at L337): research_silk_domain.md L391 records the FAO/ISA lot as "5–10 bales of 60 kg or 20 bales of 30 kg" [F, S5], so five 60-kg bales is a perfectly lawful ISA lot. The fix claims to validate "against the lot-size rule of the selected specification set" but then hard-codes only the BIS numbers into the requirement prose and blocks the ISA-legal case in its own acceptance check.

5. THE SECONDARY SUB-CLAIM IS WRONG ON ITS FACE — the reviewer says twenty-five books "is also inconsistent with the glossary's own 'twenty-two to thirty books'". The glossary (L293) gives 22–30 books per bale; 25 is mid-range, not inconsistent at any end. That sentence is self-contradicting.

6. FACT-CHECK — the reviewer's factual basis is sound and the specification already states it correctly. research_silk_domain.md L245 marks the Amendment No. 1 (Feb 2007) lot rule [F, S4], and the glossary at L343 reproduces it accurately. So the document does not overstate anything; the glossary is right and the reviewer agrees it is right. There is no unverified-fact defect here.

Residual, at most editorial and well below Major: the glossary's "Lot" entry gives the BIS grading-lot-size rule without noting that the body of the document uses "lot" in the wider sense of the submitted consignment. A half-sentence of clarification in the glossary would remove the reader's stumble. That is a Minor wording nit about one glossary line, not a contradiction in M10-05, and it is not the finding as raised — the raised finding (unlawful worked example plus a missing MUST-level blocking validation) does not stand.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part B WF-112 (approx. L1228) and OPEN-Q-B11
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The rule and its own acceptance check disagree by one. "Started at a specified opening number" means the first issued document takes 4213; the check asserts the first issued document is 4214, i.e. that 4213 is the last number already used. OPEN-Q-B11 confirms the intended semantics — "continue every existing series from its last used number" — so the rule text is the wrong one. This lands on series that WF-99 declares gap-free and statutory (money receipts, conditioning certificates, invoices). A developer who implements the rule text as written either duplicates the last paper number or leaves a permanent one-number gap that WF-102's Series Register will report as MISSING and escalate to the Unit Incharge for the life of the system.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected: The quoted text is genuine (SPEC.md L1228; authored at parts/section_2_workflow.md L786), but the claimed contradiction is a misreading that the document already resolves. The reviewer assumes "opening number" means "the first number the system issues". The specification defines it otherwise, explicitly, at SPEC.md L1425 (OPEN-Q-C4, authored at parts/section_3_functional_core.md L180): "configure each series with an opening counter value set to the legacy series' last used number, so continuity is preserved." So "opening number" is the opening COUNTER value — an opening-balance idiom for the value already consumed on paper — which makes opening = 4213 and first system-issued = 4214. That is precisely what WF-112's own acceptance check says, what OPEN-Q-B11 says six lines below it ("continue every existing series from its last used number, recorded under WF-112"), and what the locked-counter mechanism in WF-98 / M1-70 implies. Three statements agree and none contradicts; there is no off-by-one. The rule is also pinned by its acceptance check in the same table row, so a developer cannot implement the prose without reading "The first system-issued report is 4214". The claimed failure mode is additionally incoherent: WF-99's check requires the Series Register to list "every number from 1 to the current counter", so for any series continued at 4214 the numbers 1-4213 are absent regardless of the alleged off-by-one — the one-number gap is not what would drive Missing rows. (Separately and outside this finding, WF-99 / WF-102 / M1-72 do not carve out a legacy opening baseline at all, which is a genuine unraised issue.) The proposed fix is not incorrect but is redundant with OPEN-Q-C4, and its clause "cannot be edited afterwards without an audit reason" is weaker than WF-112's existing "recorded once against the series", which implies outright immutability. At most this is a Minor copy-edit: change "started at a specified opening number" to "started with a specified opening counter value" to match the vocabulary already used at L1425. Not a Major contradiction.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part C OPEN-Q-C3 (approx. L1397) and M17-40 (approx. L3811)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: This is presented as a low-stakes technical option, and M17-40 is only [SHOULD]. The research establishes the opposite: CBIC treats a statutory body as **not** being "Government", Notification 23/2021 exempts only a "government department" or local authority, CSB's PAN-level turnover has very likely exceeded ₹5 crore since FY 2017-18, and — the [VERIFIED] consequence the spec omits entirely — Rule 48(5) provides that where Rule 48(4) applies and the invoice is not issued in that manner, "such invoice shall not be treated as a valid invoice", denying the recipient input tax credit. This unit's customers are twisters, weavers, traders and exporters who do claim ITC. "Leave it switched off until the answer is in writing" means every invoice raised in the interim may be legally invalid, and the document never tells the reader that.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The finding's central factual assertion is demonstrably false. It claims the Rule 48(5) / input-tax-credit consequence is "the [VERIFIED] consequence the spec omits entirely" and that "the document never tells the reader that." The document tells the reader exactly that, 57 lines below the flagged requirement, in module M17's own open-question block at SPEC.md:3867 (authored source parts/section_4_functional_support.md:942), and again in Appendix B at SPEC.md:5851: "OPEN-Q-D21: Is the parent body within the electronic-invoicing requirement, or has it filed an exemption declaration? The research notes that the exemption is written for a 'government department' while the tax authority's own position is that a statutory body is not 'Government', which leaves a real risk that electronic invoicing applies. If it applies and is not done, the customer may be denied input tax credit — a commercial problem for a laboratory whose customers are traders and exporters. — Recommended default: build the invoice electronic-invoicing-ready per M17-40 and obtain a written answer from the parent body's tax adviser before go-live." Every element the reviewer says is missing is present: the government-department vs. statutory-body trap, the real-risk framing, ITC denial, the traders/exporters customer profile, and a written answer required before go-live. The reviewer's proposed fix is essentially a restatement of text already in the document.

The interim-invalid-invoice scenario also dissolves on context. OPEN-Q-D21 requires the written answer BEFORE GO-LIVE, so there is no window in which invoices are raised from the system without an answer. That scenario only survives if OPEN-Q-C3 is read in isolation from the module that implements it.

The terseness of OPEN-Q-C3 is deliberate document structure, not oversight. Part C is the master-data chapter and Part D the module chapter; the C-series pairs systematically with the D-series (C1 with D18 on registration number, C2 with D19/D20 on taxability and exemptions, C3 with D21), with Part D carrying the fuller reasoning. Appendix B states this: "The identifier letter shows which part raises the question."

The proposed fix is additionally misdirected. M17-40 requires only that nullable placeholder columns exist; promoting it to [MUST] has no bearing on invoice legal validity, since only actual IRP integration would. The IRP-field substance is already [MUST] elsewhere: M17-27 (every field the tax rules require), M17-41 (six-digit SAC "as required above the turnover threshold"), M17-29 (state codes and addresses).

On confidence markings (step 5), the fix would overstate rather than correct the evidence. parts/research_india_commercial.md:293 marks the Rs 5 crore threshold rule [LIKELY], and the premise that CSB's PAN-level turnover crossed it is explicitly [ASSUMPTION] ("very likely" for a 39-member board, unverified for the Board's PAN). Rule 48(5) is [VERIFIED] but its applicability is not. The reviewer's flat "This is a go-live gate, not a later question" asserts as settled a conclusion resting on an assumption the research could not confirm; the spec's hedged "real risk that electronic invoicing applies" and "may be denied input tax credit" is the more defensible phrasing and matches the document's stated discipline of not presenting unverified facts as fact (cf. OPEN-Q-D19: "This document deliberately does not state a rate as fact").

Only two cosmetic residuals exist, neither a compliance risk nor worth a change: OPEN-Q-C3 does not cross-reference OPEN-Q-D21, and the scope summary at SPEC.md:5371 describes the IRN fields as delivered scope while M17-40 is [SHOULD].

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part B §Ten corrections to the draft flow, row 10 (approx. L495); relates to M9 and OPEN-Q-C7
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Stated as a flat legal conclusion, and it overstates the clause. Clause 4.2.1 requires the laboratory to inform the customer in advance of information it intends to place in the public domain and treats other information as confidential "except for information the customer makes publicly available, or as agreed between laboratory and customer" — so publication with the customer's prior agreement is not a breach at all. The design conclusion may still be right, but it rests on the customer having not agreed, not on an absolute prohibition. Separately, the sentence sits in tension with the accreditation body's own 2021 quick-response-code circular, which the research quotes as asking for a code that lets a report be "authenticate[d] and reproduce[d] ... online" — an assessor could read the access-code gate as non-conformance. Presenting the design choice as a compliance certainty removes the lab's ability to make the choice knowingly.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted sentence exists verbatim at SPEC.md L495, but the finding is a misreading that ignores the row's own cross-reference and the module it points to.

(1) ALREADY ADDRESSED. Row 10's cell ends "(Design detail belongs to the reporting section...)". In that section, SPEC.md L2735 (M9 rules and edge cases, item 1) states the clause with exactly the caveat the reviewer says is missing: the obligation "treats all information created during laboratory activities as confidential UNLESS THE CUSTOMER HAS MADE IT PUBLIC OR AGREED OTHERWISE." The document does not assert an absolute prohibition; it states the qualified rule in the place where the design decision is actually specified.

(2) NOT AN OVERSTATEMENT IN CONTEXT. The thing row 10 corrects is a default, unconditional publication of every report to anyone who scans. Clause 4.2.1 separately requires the lab to inform the customer IN ADVANCE of information it intends to place in the public domain; a blanket publish-everything default fails that limb regardless of whether some individual customer might later agree. The reviewer's "publication with prior agreement is not a breach at all" is true in the abstract and irrelevant to the design being corrected, which contains no agreement or advance-notice mechanism.

(3) THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS FACTUALLY WRONG. "Presenting the design choice as a compliance certainty removes the lab's ability to make the choice knowingly" is contradicted by the document: M9-41 (L2699) is a full-public switch, default off, requiring Unit Incharge authorisation with recorded authoriser, date and reason plus a standing admin banner; M9-42/43 (L2700-2701) carve out the residual protections and a customer opt-out; and M9 rule 3 says in terms that this is "a deliberate, authorised, recorded decision by the Unit Incharge — not as a default that a developer chose." The clause 4.2.1 "informed in advance / as agreed" limb is also implemented as data: M1-18 (L1302), M21-68 and M21-80 (L4590, L4602 — gates publishing/analytics exports on the customer having been informed in advance), and the customer attribute "whether informed about publication of aggregate data" (L4627).

(4) THE FIX WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW CONTRADICTION. OPEN-Q-C7 in this document (L2468 and L5821) asks whether the accreditation body requires ONE verification code on the report or TWO (report vs accreditation scope). It has nothing to do with publication gating. The reviewer has confused it with item C7 of parts/research_nabl_17025.md (L645, "Public-domain intent (4.2.1)") — a different numbering scheme. The proposed sentence "confirmed under OPEN-Q-C7" would therefore create a false internal cross-reference. The fix also injects a four-sentence legal excursus into a summary table cell whose sibling cells are one-glance justifications, and duplicates L2735.

(5) THE CIRCULAR TENSION IS WEAKER THAN CLAIMED AND IS A DIFFERENT CATEGORY. parts/research_nabl_17025.md L212 and L781 already record that the 2021 circular says "should", not "shall". Its stated purpose — "prevent the manipulation of test results ... & the circulation of forged test report" — is precisely what the public tier plus the file-fingerprint check delivers (M9-18, AC-25 at L5585). Whether to name the circular and log the divergence is an omission-type observation about a non-binding "should", not an "unverified-fact-as-fact" defect, and would not be fixed by rewriting this sentence.

Residual: at most a one-word hedge ("breaches" -> "breaches, absent the customer's agreement") in a summary justification cell, already redundant given the cell's cross-reference and L2735. Not Major; too small to carry.

Incidental: the reviewer's location label "§Ten corrections to the draft flow" does not match the document — the heading is "#### 7.3 What changed, and why" and the table has 14+ rows.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part C M8-01 controlled title list (approx. L2424) versus M8-37 minimum template set (approx. L2475) and M10-29
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: M8-01 makes the title a closed controlled list and is a [MUST] against clause 7.8.2.1(a). M8-37 then mandates a go-live template set containing four document types with no matching entry in that list — Raw Silk Test Report, Twisted or Thrown Silk Yarn Test Report, Fabric or Saree Test Report, Chemical Test Report — and renames three that are in it: "Raw Silk Grading Certificate", "Preliminary Examination Report" and "Conditioned Mass (Weight) Certificate". The last two matter beyond tidiness: the research records the exact proforma headings mandated by the Indian Standard ("RECORD AND REPORT OF CONDITIONED MASS OF RAW SILK", "Record and Report of Preliminary Examination of Raw Silk") and M10-29 requires that exact title on the conditioning certificate. Whichever list the developer codes against, the other requirement fails, and there is a live risk of printing a non-standard title on the settlement document a trader's buyer cross-checks.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected: The quote is genuine (SPEC.md:2424), but the finding misreads M8-37 as a list of printed titles when the spec makes it a list of TEMPLATES. M8-37 (SPEC.md:2474) reads "Report templates exist per test family ... each recording which document type it produces. Minimum template set at go-live: ..." — the template label and the document type it produces are explicitly two different attributes. The data model confirms this is deliberate, not sloppy: `mst_report_template` (SPEC.md:5180) carries `report_type VARCHAR(40)` AND `name` as separate columns, and `txn_report` (SPEC.md:5205) carries `report_type` alongside `template_id`/`template_version`. So a template labelled "Conditioned Mass (Weight) Certificate" records report_type = the M8-01 title and prints it; nothing "fails" whichever list a developer codes against. The four allegedly unmatched entries are per-test-family layouts that all produce M8-01's generic first entry, "Test Report" — M8-37 even glosses "Raw Silk Test Report (the routine denier and limited-test format)", i.e. a format, not a title. The claimed live risk on the settlement document is not live: the exact IS proforma title is mandated twice, in M8-01 and again in M10-29 ("the title **Record and Report of Conditioned Mass of Raw Silk**", [MUST], with a print acceptance check), and no requirement anywhere instructs printing an M8-37 label as a title. The reviewer also singled out M8-37 while the same shorthand pervades the document: M1-68 (SPEC.md:1418) names series "Grading Certificate", "Weight (Conditioning) Certificate", "Preliminary Examination Report"; M10-01 uses "Weight (Conditioned Mass) Certificate"; M10-03/M10-04 use "Record and Report of Preliminary Examination" and "Preliminary Examination". A fix that renames only M8-37 leaves four other variants unaligned, which is itself evidence that these are internal shorthand labels rather than a coded contradiction. Finally, the proposed fix is actively harmful in two ways: it silently deletes "Test Certificate" from M8-01's controlled list (that title appears nowhere else in the spec, so it would cease to be an allowed title), and it promotes four template labels to mandated printed titles with no research support — research_silk_domain.md marks only the three IS proforma titles as [F, S4], and asserting "Chemical Test Report" or "Fabric or Saree Test Report" as controlled titles is an unverified addition. Residual issue is at most a Minor editorial tidiness point, well below the Major contradiction claimed.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: front_matter.md L3 and Appendix B OPEN-Q-T7 / OPEN-Q-T8, against Part B §8.3 and §10.1 and Part D M17-28
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Three parts give three different systems of record. The front matter and Appendix B (OPEN-Q-T7: "with CloudZoo as the system of record for customer identity, tax registration, invoices, receipts and assets"; OPEN-Q-T8: "CloudZoo owns customer identity, invoice, receipt, tax and asset value") state the ERP owns them. Section 2 §8.3 puts them in LIMS tables `mst_customer`, `txn_invoice`, `txn_receipt`, `mst_equipment`; §10.1 defines LIMS-issued gap-free `DVM/I/<FY4>/<5>` invoice, Money Receipt, Credit Note and Advance Receipt Voucher series; WF-99 and WF-105 make the LIMS enforce their gap-freeness and 16-character compliance; M17-28 requires the LIMS to refuse a non-compliant invoice series; M1 specifies a full Customer create/edit screen. Part D M22.1 then says the invoice series is undecided ("One or the other, never both"). The developer cannot build the customer master or the billing module until this is settled, and the two candidate answers produce entirely different schemas.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The finding rests on a misreading, and the three-way contradiction it alleges does not exist.

(1) All quotes are accurate — front_matter.md L3, appendix.md L173/174, section_5_nfr_plan.md L919/920, section_2_workflow.md §8.3/§10.1/WF-99/WF-105, section_4_functional_support.md M17-28 and M22.1 L1712 all say what the reviewer says.

(2) The central premise is wrong. §8.3 is titled "Settled vocabulary — use exactly these words", with columns "Concept | The word this project uses | Database table | Label on screen | Do not call it". It is a naming-discipline glossary and makes no system-of-record claim. The reviewer read a terminology table as an ownership declaration.

(3) Part B does not dissent — it agrees with the ERP-master position. section_2_workflow.md:65, in Part B's own corrected-flow diagram, reads "| 1  CUSTOMER  (master record, CloudZoo ERP)  |". So the part the reviewer nominates as the winning voice explicitly names CloudZoo as the customer master.

(4) The cited LIMS tables are the specified mirrors, not rival masters. M22.1 requires the LIMS to hold, for Customer identity, "Read-only copy plus LIMS-only fields"; for Tax invoice, "Master of the link from each invoice line to the specific test, and of the decision to invoice" with "ERP → LIMS to return the number, date and posted status"; for Fixed assets, "Master of the metrological record". M22-07 mandates erp_customer_id / erp_invoice_id / erp_asset_id / erp_receipt_id columns on exactly those records. The source brief tags them the same way: research_lims_reference.md:219 lists "mst_customer [ERP]" with an erp_customer_id column, and :268 lists "txn_invoice [ERP]" with erp_invoice_id. A LIMS mst_customer table is therefore the designed read-only copy plus LIMS-only fields, exactly as M22.1 prescribes — not a second system of record.

(5) Front matter, OPEN-Q-T7 and OPEN-Q-T8 are consistent with M22.1, not opposed to it. M22.1 gives ERP the master for customer identity, the posted tax invoice and its number, tax masters, inventory valuation and capitalised asset cost — which is what "owns customers, invoices, stock and assets" says. This also aligns with ARC-14 ("one system of record per field"), section_4:294 (stock valuation), OPEN-Q3/OPEN-Q-D3 (assets) and research_lims_reference.md:302.

(6) Only a narrow documentation nit survives, and it is already handled. §10.1/WF-99/WF-105/M17-28 present the invoice series as LIMS-issued without cross-referencing M22.1. But OPEN-Q36 (section_4_functional_support.md:1778) already states the decision and its default: "let CloudZoo ERP master the invoice number if its series is already compliant ... if it is not compliant, the LIMS masters the number and the ERP records it as supplied. Decide once. Never split." WF-96 additionally requires every series to be configuration with "No number format is written into program code", so both answers are the same build. The finding's claims that the developer "cannot build the customer master or the billing module" and that "the two candidate answers produce entirely different schemas" are both false — the schema is identical either way, and M22.1's third row has the counter create a provisional customer with "sample receipt is never blocked".

(7) The proposed fix is affirmatively harmful. Declaring "The LIMS is the system of record for the customer master ... the invoice, the money receipt ... and issues their number series itself" reverses M22.1's Customer identity and Tax invoice rows, contradicts OPEN-Q-T7/T8, ARC-14 and section_2_workflow.md:65, and pre-empts OPEN-Q36 — a decision the specification deliberately reserves for the Unit Incharge with the CloudZoo developer. It also deletes correct guidance from OPEN-Q-T7 on the grounds that it disagrees with M22.1, when it in fact matches it.

Severity Blocker is unsupportable: the spec's ownership model is stated once in M22.1, honoured throughout, and the single open item carries a written default.

rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The finding is a misread of the wrong artifact. The reviewer compared the generated `parts/appendix.md` against the *pre-assembly authored source* files `parts/section_1..4_*.md`, not against the assembled specification. In the actual document (`D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\SPEC.md`) there is no collision at all: `grep -c "OPEN-Q[0-9]" SPEC.md` returns 0 — every one of the 101 identifiers is lettered. A programmatic set comparison of the body (everything before the Appendix B heading) against Appendix B gives 101 IDs on each side with an exact match in both directions (appendix-minus-body = {} and body-minus-appendix = {}), so no identifier is orphaned either way.

Every cross-reference the reviewer flagged as pointing at "four candidates" in fact resolves uniquely in the assembled document: SPEC.md L112 reads "See **OPEN-Q-A1** to **OPEN-Q-A4** below."; L209 and L216 read OPEN-Q-A5; L234 reads "Registers named in OPEN-Q-A1"; L770 reads "see OPEN-Q-B5."; L4533 reads "M13 OPEN-Q-D8"; L4529 reads "M17-30, OPEN-Q-D19"; L4703 defines OPEN-Q-D36. So the Scientist-D can answer every question by number, and the two cross-references singled out in the finding are unambiguous.

The mechanism is explicit and deliberate. `D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\assemble.py` carries a per-part open-question prefix in its PARTS table (A/B/C/D, with None for section 5) and applies `t = re.sub(r"OPEN-Q(\d+)", r"OPEN-Q-%s\1" % q_prefix, t)`, which rewrites definitions and in-section cross-references in one pass. The script's own comment names the precise hazard the reviewer believes it found: "The five sections were authored independently and each numbered its own questions from 1, so OPEN-Q6 meant four different things. Prefixing per part makes every identifier unique without renumbering anything an author wrote." That comment also explains the one observation the reviewer got right — the T-series is the only prefixed series visible in the authored sources because section_5_nfr_plan.md pre-empted the merge and is assigned `None`.

The front matter is therefore accurate rather than promising a scheme the document does not use: SPEC.md L46 states the lettered convention and the delivered document follows it. Both downstream tools corroborate that the lettered namespace is canonical and machine-checked — `make_appendix.py` matches only `OPEN-Q-[A-Z]\d+` (which is why the appendix could not have been built from unlettered ids), and `lint_spec.py` L22/L70 validate against the same pattern.

The proposed fix is also not correct as a remedy: editing ~72 ids across four source files is a no-op in the output, because the assembler's regex requires a digit immediately after "OPEN-Q" and would leave a hand-written `OPEN-Q-A1` untouched. It would only defeat the documented design intent of not renumbering authored text and create four files that must be manually kept in sync with the prefix table in assemble.py.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part C M7-28 (section_3_functional_core.md L1078) against front_matter.md L15 and Part B §7.3 row 7
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The document's headline promise is two approval steps — front matter §4 "**Approval is two steps, not one.**" and Section 2 §7.3 row 7 "Two distinct steps: **technical verification** of the numbers by a competent person other than the tester, then **authorisation and signing** of the report by the Approving Authority." rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted text is real (D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\parts\section_3_functional_core.md L1078), but the claimed contradiction is a misreading of what the two cited statements assert.

1. Neither cited statement caps the number of signatures. front_matter.md L15 reads "**4. Approval is two steps, not one.** The first note had one approval..." — it sits inside a list titled "Eight changes matter more than the rest," every item of which is framed as a correction to the customer's original discussion note. The proposition is one-step -> two-step, not two-and-never-more. Section 2 §7.3 row 7 (parts\section_2_workflow.md L50) is literally a three-column "The draft note said / The corrected model says / Why it must change" table; its left cell is "'Test Log Approval' — one step by 'the authorized person'." Same comparative. I grepped for any statement asserting a cap ("exactly two", "only two signature", "no more than two", "two signatures") across all authored sections: zero hits outside the research briefs.

2. The normative floor is stated as a floor, and M7-28 does not disturb it. section_3_functional_core.md L1023 heads the subsection "**The two-step model**", and M7-01 [MUST] says "The workflow has two mandatory, separately recorded steps between result submission and report issue... There is no path from a submitted result to an issued report without both." M7-28 is [SHOULD] and is explicitly conditioned — "**Where the laboratory operates** a countersignature by the Unit Incharge" — exactly parallel to the M7 role table L1012 ("Second-level verification | Section Head | Where the laboratory operates two levels"). An optional, per-laboratory-practice configuration that adds to a mandatory floor is not a contradiction of that floor. The acceptance check "Enable three slots; all three are demanded before issue" is a test of the enabled configuration, not a claim that three are always demanded.

3. The staffing argument is self-defeating. A three-person unit does not operate a Unit Incharge countersignature, so the condition in M7-28 is never met and nothing is "unstaffable." The document handles the small-unit staffing reality head-on elsewhere: M7-05 [MUST] (the named "small-laboratory exception" with expiry, monthly count and management-review reporting) and OPEN-Q7 (section_1_foundation.md L186), whose recommended default is (b) permit-and-record. Notably OPEN-Q7 option (c) is "permit it only with a second person's countersignature" — so the countersignature capability exists precisely because the lab may choose (c), and deleting it would leave that documented option undeliverable.

4. The requirement is sourced, not invented. research_nabl_17025.md L695 item E10: "Multi-signature support: separate `reviewed_by` and `authorised_by` signature slots (7.8.1.1 + segregation of duties), and where the lab uses countersignature by the Unit Incharge, a third slot — each with its own authorisation check." M7-28 is a near-verbatim transcription of a research-brief control.

5. The proposed fix would manufacture the very contradiction it claims to remove, and is technically wrong on three counts:
   (a) It leaves M21-45 (parts\section_4_functional_support.md L1501) standing, which mandates the same third slot at **[MUST]** — a strictly stronger priority than the [SHOULD] being deleted. Post-fix, Part C would forbid what Part E mandates. M21-39 (L1495) also enumerates "countersigned by" among the stored signature meanings.
   (b) Recasting a countersignature as "a configured second-level verification under M7-09" conflates two different objects that M7-02 [MUST] explicitly separates: "Technical verification is performed per **test allocation**. Authorisation is performed per **report**." A Unit Incharge countersignature is a signature on the report; M7-09 second-level verification is a per-allocation technical check by a Section Head. The fix's own justification ("clause 7.5.1 / 7.8.2.1(o) map onto exactly two recorded identities") is a non-sequitur — those clauses set a minimum of two recorded identities, not a maximum, and M10-32 already shows the document handling a different two-block combination (Signature of Tester + authorising signatory) on the conditioning certificate, which is a template/practice matter.
   (c) It misuses the tag vocabulary. section_1_foundation.md L5 defines "[LATER]" as "deliberately deferred to a later phase and must not consume phase-1 effort." Tagging a prohibition ("No third signature slot is built in version 1") as a deferred feature is incoherent.

The residual grain of truth — that the front matter's headline does not flag the optional third slot — is a summary-altitude observation, not a contradiction, and section_1_foundation.md L5 already tells the scientist to read the module sections covering his own approval work as authoritative. Not worth a Major, or any, finding.

(Unrelated and out of scope for this finding, but noted while reading: M7-28 is [SHOULD] while M21-45 states the same slot as [MUST] — a genuine priority mismatch, and the opposite of what the reviewer alleges.)

rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
Does not stand. The quote is genuine (parts/section_1_foundation.md L9 = SPEC.md L90), and §8.4 / §7.3 row 7 say what the reviewer says they say — but the finding misreads the sentence's register and is factually wrong about reading order.

(1) READING ORDER IS BACKWARDS. The finding's whole force is that the merged model appears "in the document's opening page, where the scientist reads it first." It doesn't. SPEC.md L17, inside the section literally headed "Executive Summary — Read This First", states: "**4. Approval is two steps, not one.** The first note had one approval. A laboratory does two different things: someone technically competent **verifies**... and then the authorised signatory **authorises and signs**..." That is 73 lines BEFORE the flagged sentence. L15 likewise pre-corrects the other alleged breach: "**3. A test result is not a single number.** The first note described a 'test log entry' with observations and remarks... A single free-text 'results' box would lose exactly the data an auditor asks for." The scientist meets both corrections first.

(2) ALREADY HANDLED WITHIN PART A ITSELF, TWICE. §5 glossary: "**Verification (of a result)** | An independent check of a submitted result by a competent person other than the one who performed the test, before the report is authorised." §6.1: "**M7** | Verification and Approval | Independent checking, send-back with a coded reason, one or two levels of review, and authorisation with an electronic signature."

(3) MISREAD RHETORICAL REGISTER. The sentence sits under "### What the first note got right", in a paragraph opening "its instincts were sound", and is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the note's point 6 (appendix.md L33). Every other item in that same paragraph is likewise an instinct later refined: the "trackable unit of work with its own unique number" sentence is corrected by §7.3 row 4 (the assignable unit is the Allocation, not the sample); the QR sentence is corrected by §7.3 row 10; the equipment/stock sentence by Executive Summary point 7. Applied uniformly the reviewer's logic flags most of the paragraph — a sign of misreading, not a defect. What is endorsed is the gate (no report before checking), which §7.3 row 7 retains; row 7 changes the number of steps and people, not the gate's existence.

(4) WF-23 SCOPE OVERREAD. WF-23 binds the settled words of table 8.3 in "the user interface, ... database table and column names, ... printed documents and ... all project correspondence" — it is not a bar on the spec naming a retired artefact while describing the draft note. The document has an established convention of doing exactly that: §7.3 row 7 writes "Test Log Approval"; §7.3 row 6 writes "Tester updates the test log..."; §8.4's own "why" column says "In the draft note it means..."; §2 L7 reproduces the ERP flow verbatim including "Test Log Approval"; appendix.md L33/L55 reproduce the note verbatim. On the reviewer's reading, §8.4 and §7.3 violate WF-23.

(5) NOT THE TARGET OF THE "APPROVAL" ROW. §8.4 retires "**\"Approval\"** on its own" because the single word merges checking with signing. The sentence names both acts — "verified and approved" — so it is not the bare usage §8.4 targets. The document itself uses "Verification and Approval" as M7's official module name (SPEC.md L406, heading at L2245, and the front-matter ten-points table), so a composite naming both acts is evidently permitted.

(6) THE FIX WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW CONTRADICTION. It retains "It was right that..." and attaches the corrected two-step model, thereby crediting the original note with an insight it demonstrably lacked. appendix.md L33 reproduces the note verbatim: "The authorized person will verify and approve the test log before final report generation." §7.3 row 7 records it as "one step by 'the authorized person'", and Executive Summary point 4 says "The first note had one approval." The fix would put Part A §1 in direct conflict with all three.

At most this is a Minor editorial polish (quote the retired terms, or add a forward pointer to §7.3) — not a Major contradiction, and not worth a change that risks falsifying the historical record.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part E §26.8 Phase 6 (section_5_nfr_plan.md L699) against Part C M5-13/M5-14/M5-16 and Part B WF-22, WF-87 and §10.1 Worksheet row
