rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\parts\section_5_nfr_plan.md L703, §26.8 Phase 6), but the argument fails on its own central lever and on three of its four supports.

1) "[MUST] must therefore be in Phase 1" is a misreading of the document's stated convention. section_1_foundation.md L5 defines it explicitly: "Where the document says [MUST], the system is not finished without it. Where it says [SHOULD], it is needed but can follow shortly. Where it says [LATER], it is deliberately deferred to a later phase and must not consume phase-1 effort." [MUST] is a completeness marker, not a phase marker; [LATER] is the deferral marker. The plan is full of late [MUST]s by design: M5-03/M5-04 competency and calibration gates are [MUST] and land in Phase 3; report amendment and the ULR engine are [MUST] and land in Phase 4; M8-03 and M8-16 (subcontracted-result identification) are [MUST] and land in Phase 6 in the very same sentence the reviewer quotes. So "Part C wins because M5-16 is a [MUST]" does not follow.

2) "Phase 1 ships the high-volume test with no batch entry" is contradicted by Part C. M6-40 [MUST] (section_3_functional_core.md L923) is precisely WF-22's third clause: "A worksheet-mode grid presents many samples down the rows and readings across the columns, for the dominant case of one test performed on ten to thirty lots in one batch." M6-41 [MUST] (L924) sets the 30-lots-in-12-minutes target and states it is "tested with the actual tester before go-live" — go-live is the Phase 1 cut-over (§26.10 PLN-13, §26.13 checklist). Phase 1's Included list covers this as "the result-entry screen with raw readings, statistics and the calculation engine". The reviewer's proposed addition of "batch reading entry for many lots of one test (WF-22)" to Phase 1 is therefore already the case.

3) "No bench document in Phase 1" is contradicted by M6-46 [MUST] ("A printable blank worksheet exists... the fields match the on-screen grid exactly") and NFR-36 [MUST] ("Printed fallback forms exist for sample receipt and for each result worksheet"), both inside Phase 1's own requirement span (NFR-27 to NFR-36), with go-live checklist item 16 requiring them approved before the switch. Phase 1's bench model is scan-the-label-and-enter-on-screen (AC-03), with paper as the outage fallback.

4) "WF-87's run-level withhold is deferred to Phase 6" is false. §26.6 Phase 4 already includes "quality-control plans, control charts with configurable rules, and the withholding of release on a breach", its milestone is "fail a control check and confirm the associated customer results cannot be reported until a named person dispositions it", and AC-20 tests exactly that. The reviewer's fix would add to Phase 4 something Phase 4 already lists.

5) The §10.1 Worksheet number series row (section_2_workflow.md L735) is a numbering-master definition, not a delivery claim; Phase 1 includes "numbering series" and checklist item 4 requires every series defined. Likewise txn_worksheet exists in the schema (§25.2) from Phase 1.

What is left is a wording imprecision, not a contradiction: the Phase 6 clause reads as covering worksheets wholesale when the substance deferred is the formal blinded run sheet with typed QC positions and logged reprints (M5-15/M5-17), while cross-references to worksheets appear in Phase 1 (M6-45 "Create an offline worksheet; its number is assigned on sync") and Phase 4 (WF-87's acceptance check "Fail the check weight on a worksheet"). That is one clause of editorial tightening, Minor at most, and the document's cross-phase referencing pattern (M2-09 offering the subcontracting route in Phase 2 while subcontracting builds in Phase 6) shows it is tolerated by design.

The proposed fix is also defective as drafted: its "Leave in Phase 6 only..." list silently deletes the section 63 evidence certificate generator and the machine-readable report file from Phase 6, duplicates the QC withhold Phase 4 already owns, and moves a 12-week Phase 1 further without touching the effort table.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M3, rules and edge cases item 6 (line 539); M3-03 and its acceptance check (line 373)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: This states the domain backwards and no requirement anywhere records the lot-size rule. Under IS 15090 as amended (Amendment No. 1, February 2007) the unit of grading is one lot of 2 to 4 cartons of 30 kg each, or 1 to 2 bales of 60 kg each; and where bales differ in colour the consignment is first sorted into colour groups, each group constituting its own lot. A 20-bale consignment is therefore ten or more grading lots, each requiring its own grading certificate — the trade does not expect one certificate for 20 bales, and one certificate covering 20 bales is not a certificate the standard recognises. As written the developer will build a system that cannot express more than one lot per consignment, and the lab will issue non-conforming grading certificates that an assessor or a disputing buyer can void. M3-03's acceptance check institutionalises the error.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted text exists verbatim (parts/section_3_functional_core.md:539; M3-03 at :373), but every substantive claim fails verification.

(1) "No requirement anywhere records the lot-size rule" is false. The glossary at parts/section_1_foundation.md:262 states: "Lot | The unit of raw-silk grading; under the current amended Indian Standard, two to four cartons of 30 kg each, or one to two bales of 60 kg each" — carried straight from the [F, S4]-marked brief line at parts/research_silk_domain.md:245.

(2) "One certificate covering 20 bales is not a certificate the standard recognises" is false for this laboratory's actual grading work. parts/research_silk_domain.md marks the FAO/ISA variant [F, S5]: "lot 5-10 bales of 60 kg or 20 bales of 30 kg". parts/section_1_foundation.md:27 records that the unit's non-Limited-test volume is "a small number of full ISA gradings", and ISA grading is a separately priced catalogue record (M1-28). A 20-bale lot producing one grading certificate is exactly the ISA lot. Item 6 cites no standard, so it is not "the domain backwards"; it is the ISA case, and its actual teaching (sub-units are not samples) is correct.

(3) "The developer will build a system that cannot express more than one lot per consignment" is false. M3-01 defines one Test Request to many Samples, "one per physical item or lot received"; M3-15 [MUST] bulk-registers 40 bales as 40 samples in one grid ("not 40 forms"); M3-17 handles received-vs-requested mismatches; M8-38 and the M3 report-grouping table (Options A/B/C, lines 522-528) already support one report per sample; NFR-02 (parts/section_5_nfr_plan.md:44) times registering "a batch of 30 lots ... for the same customer". Ten lot samples on one Test Request, each with its own number, allocations and certificate, is the model as written. M3-03 is a generic "has sub-units" requirement spanning bales, books, skeins, bobbins, cones and pieces; it does not cap a request at one lot and institutionalises nothing.

The proposed fix would also introduce a new error and a new contradiction. It asserts that each colour group "constitut[es] its own lot"; the [F, S4, cl.3.3] brief line (research_silk_domain.md:257) says the opposite — all bales sorted out for grading constitute a lot, and where a lot is split into groups the skein draw is proportional to the books in each group. The spec already implements that correct reading in M10 (the "Bales sorted by colour into groups" and "Colour group detail" fields at lines 1615-1616, and M10 rule 6 at line 1673), so the fix would contradict M10. The proposed M3-34 hard block at request confirmation would additionally collide with ISA-method grading, with M3-15, with M10-05's "one or more" bale validation, and with M3 rule 1 (sample arrives before the request is complete).

What survives is cosmetic, not a Blocker: item 6 and M3-03's acceptance check say "lot" unqualified, where the document's own terminology table (parts/section_2_workflow.md:550) asks that the IS unit be written "Grading Lot". That is a wording nit, not a compliance risk.

rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The module that exists to produce an exact settlement number never writes down a single formula. "Computed from the net mass and the average moisture content" has two common implementations that give different answers, because "moisture content" (loss ÷ wet mass) and "moisture regain" (loss ÷ dry mass) are different quantities and M10 uses the words "moisture" and "regain" in adjacent requirements without defining either. On a 60 kg net bale at 8 per cent, D = 60 × 0.92 = 55.200 kg gives a conditioned weight of 61.272 kg, while D = 60 ÷ 1.08 = 55.556 kg gives 61.667 kg — a 0.4 kg difference per bale, roughly ₹1,500 of raw silk, in a document produced precisely so that neither party has to trust the other's arithmetic. M10-19 has the same defect for the set moisture percentage. A solo developer will guess, and the guess will not be visible until a customer audits a certificate.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (SPEC.md:2814 = parts/section_3_functional_core.md:1569), and it is true that M10-22 does not transcribe an algebraic expression. But the finding's central claim — that the document leaves the wet-basis/dry-basis choice open, so "a solo developer will guess" — is wrong on three independent counts.

1. THE DOCUMENT ALREADY PINS THE FORMULA DOWN, WITH A WORKED EXAMPLE THAT ONLY RECONCILES ONE WAY. parts/section_2_workflow.md:391-392 (SPEC.md:833-834), in the section whose stated purpose is establishing shared vocabulary, defines the Weight/Conditioning Certificate as "...conditioned mass (oven-dry mass plus 11 %)" and gives: "gross 60.4 kg, tare 1.6 kg, net 58.8 kg, average moisture 7.2 %, oven-dry 54.57 kg, conditioned weight 60.57 kg." I ran both interpretations:
   - moisture content (wet basis), D = 58.8 x (1 - 0.072) = 54.5664 -> 54.57; C = x1.11 = 60.5687 -> 60.57. Both printed figures match exactly at the stated 2 dp.
   - moisture regain (dry basis), D = 58.8 / 1.072 = 54.8507 -> 54.85; C = 60.8843 -> 60.88. Both figures fail.
   Also 60.4 - 1.6 = 58.8, so the tare chain is internally consistent. The example is a formula specification by substituted values, and it selects precisely the interpretation the reviewer says is missing. It matches the [F]-verified research source: parts/research_silk_domain.md:212 gives "Oven-dry mass D = M_n(1 - m/100) -> Conditioned weight of the bale = 1.11 D", and line 178 marks the 11% regain [F, S4 and S5]. So the reviewer's own proposed formula is the one the document already implies — this is a redundancy, not a defect.

2. M10-23 IS MISREAD; IT IS NOT AMBIGUOUS. The finding lists M10-23 as having "the same defect." M10-23 (line 1570) reads "...computed by adding the official regain allowance to the oven-dry mass. The regain rate is held as configuration..., seeded at eleven percent of the oven-dry mass." The base of the percentage is stated twice, explicitly. C = D + 0.11D = 1.11D admits no second reading. M10-24 further requires the definition of conditioned mass to print on the certificate face. The reviewer's replacement for M10-23 says exactly what M10-23 already says.

3. "THE GUESS WILL NOT BE VISIBLE UNTIL A CUSTOMER AUDITS A CERTIFICATE" IS FALSE. M10-27 requires stored test vectors "taken from historical manual conditioning worksheets, which the system re-runs automatically on every software release... This is the validation evidence for the calculation," with the acceptance check "every historical certificate's conditioned weight reproduces exactly, including rounding." M10 rule 8 mandates twenty completed manual worksheets as a pre-go-live regression suite, and NFR-41 (section_5_nfr_plan.md:115) requires 100% match on at least 20 historical worksheets, re-run every release, as ISO/IEC 17025 clause 7.11.2 validation evidence. A wet/dry mix-up is a ~0.5-0.7% error on every single bale; it would fail all twenty vectors on the first run, months before any customer sees a certificate. The specific harm scenario the Blocker severity rests on is engineered out by three separate requirements.

Additionally, M1-46, M1-48 and M14-07 establish that calculation formulae are deliberately held as versioned master data with test vectors rather than written into requirement prose. M10 describing the derivation while the expression lives in configuration is consistent with the document's design, not an oversight.

RESIDUAL MERIT (not blocker-grade): the section 1 glossary (section_1_foundation.md:267) defines "Moisture regain" as a dry-weight percentage but carries no "Moisture content" entry, and M10 uses both words. A reader of M10 plus the glossary alone could momentarily conflate them. Adding a one-line glossary entry for moisture content, or the substituted formula to M10-22, would be a cheap clarity win. That is a Minor editorial improvement, not a buildability blocker.

FIX PROBLEM: beyond being largely redundant, the proposed addition to M10-02 ("The column holding m is named moisture_content_percent") pushes a physical column name into a requirements row that elsewhere defers physical schema to the section 25 data model in section_5_nfr_plan.md — and that data model contains no conditioning/weight-certificate tables at all (I checked; there is no txn_conditioning_* entry). Naming one column there, in isolation, mixes abstraction levels and would sit oddly against the rest of the schema treatment.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M6, rules and edge cases item 4 (line 990); no requirement ID in M6, M7 or M8 implements it
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The single hardest rule in raw-silk grading exists in this specification only as a prose note with no requirement ID, no priority tag, no acceptance check and no stated threshold. The standard's rule is explicit: where conditioned size differs from the size marked on the bales by more than 7 per cent either way, the results of all tests except the conditioned size test shall be discarded, all tests including conditioned size shall be repeated taking the conditioned size result as the basis, and the grading certificate shall be issued from the repeat tests. Nothing in M1's data model, M6's result states, M7's verification or M8's issue path provides a Discarded state, a superseded_by link between test runs, a block on verifying discarded results, or a rule that the certificate must be built from the repeat run. As written, M7 will verify and M8 will sign a grading certificate built from results the governing standard requires to be thrown away, and the developer has no way to know the number 7 exists.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected: The quoted text exists (parts/section_3_functional_core.md:990, SPEC.md:2235), but the central claim is false. The reviewer searched only the M-module sections; the document places state machines and cross-module transition rules in the workflow section (SPEC.md:1013 states this explicitly). The rule is fully specified there: WF-74 [MUST] (parts/section_2_workflow.md:683, SPEC.md:1125) reads "Where the specification set is BIS and the conditioned-size result differs from the declared size marked on the bales by more than 7 % either way, the system discards every other allocation on that sample, creates repeat allocations for all of them including conditioned size, and prevents the certificate being issued from the discarded run", with the acceptance check "Enter a conditioned size 9 % away from the declared size. All sibling allocations move to Discarded, repeats are created, and the report compiler refuses the discarded results." So the requirement ID, the [MUST] tag, the 7 % threshold and the acceptance check all exist. SPEC.md:1049 defines the Allocation state Discarded, naming IS 15090 and the 7 % rule, with actions "Records the discard reason and the triggering allocation. Creates a repeat allocation in Pending, linked as a retest of this one" — that is the Discarded state and the superseded_by-equivalent link. SPEC.md:1071 states "certificate issued from the repeat run only". SPEC.md:2535 (M8 report field table) restricts report composition to "Only Verified allocations selectable", and Discarded is a terminal state, so discarded results can be neither verified nor reported. All three proposed requirements therefore duplicate existing normative text, and M6-51 would actively weaken WF-74 by converting the standard's fixed 7 % into a general configurable tolerance. Provenance also checks out: research_silk_domain.md:402 and :430 mark the 7 % rule [F, S4] (verified). Two Minor residual nits exist but are different findings from the one raised: M1-75 (SPEC.md:1432) omits a discard reason-code group from its fifteen seeded groups even though the Discarded state requires a recorded reason; and the state table lists Discarded only as an onward transition from Verified, while WF-74 discards every sibling allocation regardless of its current state.

rejectedForTheRecord.problem: This models evenness backwards and destroys the raw record. The observation for evenness is a count of stripes on each of the 20 seriplane panels (2 panels from each of the 10 bobbins); Evenness variation I, II and III are classifications derived from those counts against the grade table. Making the tester pick a band (a) collapses 20 raw readings into one judgement, which M6-01 expressly forbids and which the standard's own per-part proforma requires to be recorded, (b) makes the classification a typed value, contradicting M6 rules item 3 and M1-51 which insist the grade is computed from data, (c) leaves M7-14's recompute action nothing to recompute, and (d) makes Evenness III, an auxiliary characteristic that lowers the grade by class differences, unauditable. Neatness genuinely is a picker; evenness is not, and the requirement conflates the two.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is real (parts/section_3_functional_core.md:872), but every consequence the reviewer draws from it is refuted by the immediate context, and the reviewer's own domain premise is backwards relative to the document's research brief.

1. "Collapses 20 raw readings into one judgement, which M6-01 expressly forbids." M6-09 governs the *input control type* for enumerated parameters, not storage or cardinality. M6-01 (line 864, eight rows above in the same table) is unqualified: "Every parameter's readings are stored as individual reading rows... never collapsed into a single stored average." M6-02/M6-03 enforce the required reading count from the method master for every parameter. The M6 field table (line 969) settles it explicitly: "Raw reading value (per row) | Decimal (18,6) **or enumerated** or text | Yes to the required count | ... enumerated values restricted". Enumerated is a per-reading-row value type, so a picker is fully compatible with 20 panel rows. The exact same mechanism already demonstrably works for neatness: M6-09 makes neatness a picker, and M6-06's acceptance check is "Compute low neatness on twenty panels; the system averages the worst four." A picker plainly does not mean one collapsed reading anywhere in this module.

2. "Makes the classification a typed value, contradicting M6 rules item 3 and M1-51." "Classification bands" cannot be read as the grade (4A...E). M6 rules item 3 (line 989) says "Grade is computed, never entered. No tester ever types '3A'," and the field table (line 979) has "Computed grade | Derived | Auto | Read-only; **never typed**." An ambiguous phrase is pinned down by two explicit rules in the same module. M6-09 says nothing about grade at all; M1-51 is untouched.

3. "Leaves M7-14's recompute action nothing to recompute" and "makes Evenness III unauditable." Both follow only from claim 1, which is false. The reading rows exist per M6-01/M6-02, M6-05 stores intermediates, and Evenness III's auxiliary class-difference role is grade-engine configuration under M1-51(b)(e)(f) — nothing in M6-09 touches it.

4. The reviewer's domain premise is inverted. research_silk_domain.md:401 [F, S4, S5] states the evenness result is "stripe counts bucketed into **I / II / III**", and line 99 "number of stripes per 20 panels, split into Evenness I / II / III". section_2_workflow.md:352 and the brief's grade-computation row confirm evenness I and II are *major test parameters* and evenness III an *auxiliary parameter*, each of which maps into a grade band. So Evenness I/II/III ARE the observations/counts; the derived thing is the grade. The reviewer asserts the opposite — "Evenness variation I, II and III are classifications derived from those counts against the grade table" — and builds the fix on it.

5. The proposed fix is therefore affirmatively wrong and would inject new contradictions. (a) It makes Evenness I/II/III "computed classifications... read-only", contradicting section_2_workflow.md:352 and M1-51, where evenness I/II are graded major parameters and evenness III an auxiliary parameter. (b) "one reading per seriplane panel" / "Enter 20 stripe counts" is information-losing: a single integer per panel cannot be bucketed into three severity classes, so the tester's class-I/II/III judgement against the Official Standard Variation Photographs is destroyed — the very audit loss the finding claims to prevent. (c) It puts "cleanness defect classes (super-major, major, minor **counts** per panel)" under the enumerated picker, i.e. makes counts non-numeric, contradicting its own stated principle and M6-06 ("cleanness percentage from weighted defect **counts**"). (d) "2 per bobbin" appears only in research_silk_domain.md:385, never in the specification.

The only defensible residue is a wording nit, not a Blocker contradiction: M6-09 spells out the full permitted value set for neatness and for the visual/tactual ratings but leaves evenness as "the classification bands" without naming them, and "bands" is loose because the document uses "grade band" elsewhere (M1-50, section_2_workflow.md:352). That is largely handled already by M1-43, which holds "permitted enumerated values where applicable" as parameter-master configuration rather than spec prose.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M6-13 (line 881); M1-77 (line 189); nothing in M1–M10 implements the analysis
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The specification states the purpose of the mandatory equipment identifier and then never requires the capability. M1-77 offers "equipment later found out of calibration" as an amendment reason and M8-58 opens a nonconformity when it is used, but nothing produces the list of affected work: given a balance that fails its calibration on the 20th with the last good check on the 1st, no screen tells the lab which readings, which allocations, which verified results, which issued reports and which conditioned-mass certificates were produced on that instrument in between. In a unit doing 11,000 tests a year on a handful of instruments, that list is hundreds of documents and cannot be reconstructed by hand. This is the standard's nonconforming-work requirement, it is the first thing an assessor asks to see after a failed calibration, and the developer has no requirement to build it.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted text is genuine (SPEC.md line 2126, M6-13), but the claimed omission is false. The reviewer scoped their search to modules M1–M10 and concluded the capability is absent from the specification. Their own finding admits the limit: "nothing in M1–M10 implements the analysis." That is true and by design — equipment lifecycle control lives in M11, and the capability is specified there in more detail than the proposed fix.

M11-24 [MUST] (line 2976) is titled "OUT-OF-CALIBRATION IMPACT ANALYSIS" and requires a one-action function that (a) proposes a `suspect_from` date defaulting to the last known-good calibration or intermediate check, (b) lists every test, sample, worksheet, issued report and customer that used the instrument in the window, (c) requires a named authorised person to disposition each affected issued report as Not affected (with technical justification) / Retest / Amend report / Withdraw and replace, (d) records disposition, reason, person and date, (e) drives customer notification and recall, and (f) links the exercise to a Nonconformity record. Its acceptance check is the reviewer's own scenario: a failed balance calibration across 40 tests, 12 reported; the analysis must list exactly those and cannot be closed while any report is un-dispositioned.

The three specific sub-claims each fail:
1. "No screen tells the lab..." — M11.1 (line 2941) lists an "Impact Analysis" screen for Lab In-Charge and Quality Manager, whose stated purpose is to list every result and report produced by an instrument in a chosen window and disposition each.
2. "...which allocations..." — line 1072's exception table uses the reviewer's exact vocabulary: "Instrument found out of calibration after work was done | Nonconformity -> impact analysis lists every allocation and report that used it -> per-report disposition -> affected allocations Invalidated and reports amended or replaced."
3. "...and which conditioned-mass certificates" — line 825 defines the data model: "Test report, grading certificate, conditioned-mass certificate, pre-shipment certificate and HSN certificate are all report types — one entity, different templates." Conditioned-mass certificates are therefore inside M11-24's "issued report" set by construction, not outside it.

The capability is also load-bearing across the document, not an isolated mention: goal 6 (line 172) makes it a headline acceptance criterion ("When an instrument or a consumable lot is found faulty, the affected work is listed automatically"); M11-25 requires the list be produced by a database query on the mandatory equipment reference rather than a manual search, with identical repeat runs; M11-12 and M11-17 auto-offer the analysis on a failed calibration and a failed intermediate check; line 3072 extends it to the silently-lapsed-calibration case; M12-12 covers the reviewer's consumable/reference-material lot case (BATCH IMPACT ANALYSIS); line 3471 extends the pattern to formula versions; M15-29 makes an impact analysis on previous results mandatory on every Nonconformity; DB-20 (line 5278) makes `equipment_id` and `consumable_lot_id` NOT NULL specifically so the analysis is one query; `txn_ncr_affected` (line 5221) is the storage table; line 4014 alerts when an impact analysis stays open; RACI rows exist for "Impact analysis — run" and "— disposition" (lines 4329-4330); and master acceptance tests 15 and 16 (lines 4490-4491) plus AC-18 (line 5573) test it end to end. AC-18 is nearly verbatim the reviewer's proposed acceptance check, including the last-known-good-check framing and the four disposition outcomes.

The proposed fix is also independently wrong and would inject two real contradictions. Its disposition set ("no action needed, amend, or withdraw") drops Retest, conflicting with M11-24(c) and AC-18's four-outcome vocabulary and with `disposition VARCHAR(25)`. And "one nonconforming-work record is opened per affected document" directly contradicts M11-24(f), which links the whole exercise to a single Nonconformity, and contradicts the `txn_ncr_affected` schema, where one `ncr_id` fans out to many affected rows. Adding M6-54 would duplicate M11-24 in a module that does not own equipment lifecycle, with divergent semantics.

Two minor citation defects also undercut the finding: M1-77 is at line 1434, not line 189, and the reviewer's characterisation of M8-58 as the end of the trail ignores that M8-58 opens the nonconformity that M15-29 then requires an impact analysis on.

The only residue worth anything is editorial: M6-13 asserts the purpose of the mandatory equipment identifier without pointing the reader to M11-24. M6 does cross-reference other modules elsewhere (M6-19 cites "the sub-sample tree from M4"), so a "(see M11-24)" pointer would match house style. That is a Minor cross-reference nit, not a missing capability and nowhere near a Blocker, so the finding as filed does not stand.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M6-02 (line 865) against M6-21 (line 894)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The specification never says whether the required count is evaluated on entered rows or on included rows, and M6-21 makes exclusion permanent (a reading is never deleted). Both readings of the rule are wrong in a different way. Counting entered rows means a tester enters 40 sizing-skein weights, excludes 3 as specimen defects, and submits an average size and standard deviation resting on 37 individually weighed skeins — which the method does not permit and which M7's checklist will not catch, because item (b) only asks whether exclusions are within the permitted count and carry reasons. Counting included rows blocks submission forever, because the excluded row cannot be deleted and the specification gives a replacement reading no reading number to occupy. A developer must guess, on the parameter that carries 40 or 80 readings.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is verbatim (D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\parts\section_3_functional_core.md:865, assembled at SPEC.md:2110), but both of the reviewer's "wrong in a different way" branches fail against the document.

(1) "The specification gives a replacement reading no reading number to occupy" is false. The replacement mechanism exists under a different name — `supersedes_observation_id`. WF-9 (SPEC.md:701): "A correction is a new observation row plus an exclusion marker and a mandatory reason on the original." DB-06 (SPEC.md:5264): "The raw readings in `txn_observation` are never updated: a correction is a **new observation row** whose `supersedes_observation_id` points at the old one, and the old one gets `is_excluded = true` with a reason." DB-33 (SPEC.md:5298) permits exactly one update to that table, setting `is_excluded`. Decisively, the `txn_observation` unique constraint (SPEC.md:5200, 6th column of the 25.2 table) is `sample_test_id, parameter_id, reading_no, supersedes_observation_id` — the discriminator is in the key precisely so a replacement re-uses the *same* `reading_no` as the row it supersedes. So the "blocks submission forever" branch collapses: non-deletion is irrelevant because the replacement is an append, and the schema is built for it.

(2) The "entered rows" branch is not left to a developer's guess, and it is not uncontrolled. M6-22 (SPEC.md:2140) bounds it: "Exclusion of a reading beyond a configurable count or percentage requires the Section Head's authorisation", acceptance check "Exclude a fourth reading from forty with a limit of three; authorisation is demanded." M7-36(c) (SPEC.md:2341) treats "an excluded reading beyond the permitted count" as a bar to bulk verification, i.e. reported results routinely and legitimately carry exclusions within the permitted count. The reviewer quotes M7-12(b) and dismisses it, but the per-method permitted exclusion count *is* the control that decides how many determinations may be dropped, with Section Head escalation above it and M7-13 pre-filling reading counts as evidence.

(3) The premise "which the method does not permit" is unsupported. parts\research_silk_domain.md:383 confirms 40/80 individually weighed sizing skeins [F, S4] but says nothing about a prohibition on computing on fewer, and no brief states a minimum acceptable count. M6-21's own reason pick-list includes "statistical outlier per the method's own rule", i.e. the spec already assumes methods may prescribe exclusion; research_silk_domain.md:107 shows minimums are data ("in-house (5 skeins min)").

(4) The proposed fix would introduce two new contradictions. "Excluding a reading re-opens the shortfall and blocks submission until a replacement reading is entered" makes M6-22, M7-12(b) and M7-36(c) dead letters — no submitted result could ever contain an unreplaced exclusion, so there is nothing for a "permitted count" of exclusions or Section Head authorisation to govern. And "a replacement takes the next unused reading number" directly contradicts DB-06 and the `txn_observation` unique key, and breaks the M6 field table's "Reading number (per row) | Integer | Auto | Sequential from 1 | Read-only" (SPEC.md:2213), M5-16's printed worksheet with "blank spaces sized for the readings", and M6-35's "Enter on the last reading of a parameter advances to the first reading of the next parameter". The fix also mandates that a replacement "carries its own specimen identifier", but `txn_observation` has no specimen column (specimen is captured per activity — M6-19 and the field table's "Specimen / sub-sample used | Lookup (multi)"), so it silently demands a schema change it does not name.

What remains is at most editorial: M6-02, WF-14 (SPEC.md:706) and WF-70 (SPEC.md:1121) all say "at least the required number of readings" without spelling out in that one sentence that the count is satisfied by reading rows present. That is resolvable — and resolved in one direction only — by M6-22 / M7-12(b) / M7-36(c), which any developer building result entry must read. Not a Major buildability blocker.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M5-18 (line 736) against M5-21 (line 739), M5-23 (line 741), M5-12 (line 720) and M7-05 (line 1030)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The specification never says whether the data-layer filter is keyed on the user's set of roles or on the screen and record being served, and in this unit the difference decides whether blinding exists at all. M5-21 makes blinding per role and per section, M5-23 exempts verifiers entirely, M8 gives the report writer normal access, and M5-12 and M7-05 both acknowledge that one person in a three-person unit holds several of these roles. Under the ordinary implementation — permissions as the union of a user's roles — the moment the tester is also a verifier or report writer the data layer must return the customer name, and M5-18's guarantee silently evaporates for precisely the people it targets, while M5-20's "search the customer name as a tester; no results" becomes untestable. This is not a policy question the developer can resolve alone.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (D:\Prashant_WorkSpace\TTL Software\parts\section_3_functional_core.md line 736 = SPEC.md line 1981), and the cited line numbers all check out. But the central claim — "the specification never says whether the data-layer filter is keyed on the user's set of roles or on the screen and record being served" — is false on three independent counts, and the proposed fix would contradict four other requirements.

1. THE KEYING IS SPECIFIED, AND IT IS ROLE/PERMISSION-KEYED, NOT CONTEXT-KEYED. M21-15 (SPEC.md line 4386) states the rule in exactly the terms the reviewer says are missing: "For roles without the *view customer identity* permission, the customer name, address ... shall be **absent from the data returned by the system**, not merely hidden in the display." The database section pins the same mechanism down to a named permission code: `sys_permission` — "Atomic permission, including `customer.view_identity` which is how the blinding rule is implemented" (line 5238). The M21.3 permission matrix grants it per role column — "Customer master — view identity | R | – | R | R | R | R | R | – | R | R own" (line 4285) — and even defines a dedicated matrix mark for masked reads: "**M** read with customer identity masked" (line 4283). M5-21 and M21-22 both say blinding is configurable "per role and per section". The M5 field-level blinding table's columns are roles. Every one of these is role-keyed. A developer has an unambiguous implementation: a permission held (or not) via the user's roles. The reviewer's own "ordinary implementation — permissions as the union of a user's roles" is not an accidental gap; it is the specified design.

2. THE MULTI-ROLE COLLISION IS ADDRESSED AT THE EXACT POINT THE REVIEWER SAYS IT IS SILENT. The M5 "unavoidable cases" table, twelve lines below M5-18 (SPEC.md line 2036), contains a row devoted to this scenario: "**The tester also writes reports in a small unit** | Report generation requires the customer | Report generation is a separate role with normal access. Where one person holds both roles, the overlap is recorded per M5-12." So the guarantee does not "silently evaporate" — the document names the case, states that the second role carries normal (unblinded) access, and specifies the mitigation: record the overlap. The same policy is stated at M5-12, M7-05, M13-10 ("record the overlap on the test and on the report so the laboratory can defend it and count how often it happens", line 3263), and §3322 "The single-scientist problem ... The system must not pretend otherwise." M5-25 (line 2041) makes the choice explicit and binding: the software "must **not** be described, in the interface or in its documentation, as making blinding absolute." The reviewer has rediscovered a limitation the document deliberately documents and refuses to overclaim.

3. M5-20 IS NOT UNTESTABLE. Its check reads "Search the customer name **as a tester**"; the fixture is an account holding the Tester role, which is a valid and reproducible test account (M21-01 requires per-person logins but places no bar on single-role accounts). AC-07 (line 5552) uses the same single-role framing. At worst the check does not cover the multi-role case — a coverage gap in one acceptance check, not an untestable requirement.

4. THE PROPOSED FIX WOULD INTRODUCE REAL CONTRADICTIONS, one of them serious. (a) "keyed on the pair (screen context, allocation), never on the union of the signed-in user's roles" directly contradicts M21-15, M21-22, M5-21, the M21.3 matrix and the `customer.view_identity` permission design — it would require rewriting the entire access-control model in M21 and the DB section. (b) Far worse, the fix's final clause — "unblinded data only ... for allocations they did not enter" and "the same account entering the result cannot open the verification context for it" — flatly contradicts M7-05 and M13-10, which require the system to *permit* self-verification under a time-boxed, named-method exception approved by the Unit Incharge. M7-05's acceptance check ("Enable the exception for one method for one month; self-verification is then permitted, recorded, counted, and blocked again after expiry") would become unsatisfiable. (c) "the customer identity fields are absent from the response irrespective of their other roles" reasserts precisely the absolute guarantee M5-25 forbids.

The only residual point with any merit is that no single sentence says "permissions are the union of the user's roles" in so many words. That is a documentation nicety, union is the universal RBAC default, and line 2036 confirms the consequence is understood and accepted — trivial, not Major. The finding does not stand.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M4-02 (line 580) against M3-15 (line 395) and the M5 blinding table row "Receipt photographs" (line 772)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Two separate collisions. First, throughput: M3-15 requires 40 samples to be registered in one grid in under three minutes, about 4.5 seconds a row, which cannot include staging and shooting a numbered photograph; at roughly 11,000 samples a year, 98 per cent of them a ₹50 test arriving in daily batches of 10 to 30 lots, this is 30 to 45 individually staged photographs a day for one counter clerk, and it will be the first rule abandoned. Second, blinding: the table says receipt photographs are visible to a tester only after the customer's marks are "masked or the image is cropped", but no requirement creates that derivative, names who produces it or provides a tool, and M4-03 forbids replacing a photograph. The only ways to satisfy both are a manual crop per sample, 11,000 times a year in a three-person unit, or letting the tester see the marks.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted text is verbatim (SPEC.md:1825), but both claimed collisions are misreadings.

(1) Throughput. M4-02 gates ACCEPTANCE; M3-15 measures REGISTRATION, and the document explicitly separates the two steps: M3-20 (SPEC.md:1652) "A barcode label is printed ... at the moment of acceptance, not at registration"; the M3 field table (SPEC.md:1743) "Starts the clock at acceptance, not here" and "Sample state ... Set by M4"; WF-32 (Expected -> Received) and WF-34 (Received -> Accepted) are separate MUST transitions (SPEC.md:1087-1090). "Register 40 samples in one grid in under three minutes; all 40 appear with distinct numbers" creates 40 records in state Received/Expected and never had to include photography. WF-22 (:714), NFR-02 (:4760), NFR-18 (:4785) are all worded around registration too. Only AC-02 (:5542, "30 labels queue ... under 12 minutes") pulls acceptance in via M3-20, and there the 24 s/lot budget is already strained by M4-01's eleven-item checklist and M4-04's calibrated weighing independent of the photograph, so the photograph is not the identifiable culprit. No contradiction with the cited requirement.

(2) Blinding. The claim "no requirement creates that derivative, names who produces it" is false. The M5 unavoidable-cases table (SPEC.md:2031) assigns it: "the clerk must (a) photograph the sample with the marks, storing that image at Section Head visibility; ... (c) over-label the sample ... Where the mark cannot be covered ... the clerk records 'identity not maskable'." The blinding row (:2017) is a permission gate, not a mandate to produce a derivative -- absent a masked version the tester sees no photograph. The reviewer's "only two ways" is a false dichotomy omitting the document's actual default. No requirement obliges a tester to see a receipt photograph: the tester gets "Condition on receipt and deviations | Visible" (:2016), and report inclusion is optional and done by the non-blinded report role ("Sample photograph included | Yes / No + selection | No", :2556; :2036). research_gap_analysis.md:512 confirms the intent was Tier-1 storage with no derivative. The M4-03 argument is inverted: "a corrected photograph is an additional photograph" (:1826) explicitly PERMITS a masked derivative alongside the untouched original.

(3) The proposed fix would create two new collisions. A batch photograph with "every item ... legible in the frame" is unachievable against NFR-117 (:4985, images "compressed to at most 200 kilobytes each ... still adequate to read a bale mark") -- 200 KB cannot resolve thirty labels. And "at least one bench image ... for any sample whose tester view is blinded" applies to every sample under M5, so on top of the M5-mandated marks image it doubles the per-sample shot count the fix set out to reduce. It also leaves WF-33 unamended.

Separate genuine defect the reviewer did not find (worth raising on its own): WF-33 (SPEC.md:1088, MUST) requires a photograph only "where any checklist item is adverse", with an acceptance check exercising only the adverse branch, while M4-02 (:1825, MUST) is unconditional; WF-33 also places it at Received while M4-02 places it before Accepted. Two MUSTs disagree on conditionality and timing. That is a real contradiction, but it is not the finding under review.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M3 worked example (lines 505–530); the Limited test is mentioned once in the whole section, in a parenthesis in M8-37 (line 1230)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The one worked example the document says "the specification must settle" is an ISA-grading-shaped job, which the research puts at 0.6 per cent of the unit's work, while the Limited test at 98.0 per cent of 11,294 samples is never specified anywhere in M1–M10: not its composition (winding, wrap-reel of sizing skeins at 225 m for cottage basin or 450 m for multi-end, manual kilcha, denier and size deviation), not its twenty weighings to one lot result, not its five-skein minimum, not its report shape, not the daily batch of 10 to 30 lots it arrives in. A developer building against this section will design, demonstrate and acceptance-test the rare case and discover the dominant one after go-live, and the scientist reading it has no way to check that the system fits the work actually done.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (parts/section_3_functional_core.md:507 = SPEC.md:1752), and the reviewer's raw word-count is correct: the string "Limited test" appears only once in section 3. But the inference drawn from it is a misreading, because the document deliberately names the 98 % case by other words, and every capability the finding calls missing is specified — most of it inside M1-M10.

The dominant batch shape has its own MUST requirements with acceptance checks in M1-M10: M3-15 bulk registration grid (40 samples, one screen, one save, under three minutes); M6-40 "worksheet-mode grid ... for the dominant case of one test performed on ten to thirty lots in one batch"; M6-41 speed target "for the dominant test" (one lot under twenty seconds, thirty lots under twelve minutes, acceptance-tested with the real tester); M7-36 bulk verification with the acceptance check "Bulk-verify thirty routine size tests"; M7 rule 8 ("Eleven thousand samples a year of one routine test cannot be verified one screen at a time"). The recommendation printed immediately below the disputed example (line 528) reasons explicitly from the dominant case: "the research shows Dharmavaram's dominant work is a high-volume, low-value test done in daily batches of ten to thirty lots." So the section does not present the five-hank job as representative; the example is scoped by its own heading to the structural question it settles (1 request : 5 samples : 15 allocations, and the report-grouping choice), which a single-test batch example cannot settle.

Each itemised sub-claim fails: (a) composition - parts/section_1_foundation.md:260 defines the Limited test as "winding, wrap-reeling of sizing skeins, kilcha making, and denier with deviation - accounting for about 98 per cent of Dharmavaram's samples", with kilcha defined at :259 and modelled as a specimen node (M4-10 arbitrary-depth sub-sample tree, acceptance check "Build a five-level tree from a lot down to a sizing skein"); (b) 225 m vs 450 m - parts/section_4_functional_support.md:545 (M14 rules item 2) names that exact local deviation and requires either a separate in-house method version with a validation record or a formal deviation under M14-16, and M3-07 records the reeling device as affecting "the effective test recipe and the price"; (c) twenty weighings to one lot result - M1-36 "required reading counts" and "sample draw rule", M1-45 "number of readings required", M6-03 (count resolved from the method master, not typed), M6-06 (size deviation as a configured computed value), plus V7 = 20 readings and AC-03 "enters 20 readings using only the keyboard"; (d) five-skein minimum - M1-29 "minimum chargeable quantity", M1-26 sample-type minimum quantity, the M3 registration rule "warn if below the sample type minimum", M3 rule 4; (e) report shape - M8-37 names "Raw Silk Test Report (the routine denier and limited-test format)" in the go-live template set, M8-38 defaults to one consolidated report, and PLN-02 forbids guessing it while a real specimen exists ("a Limited Test report ... Photograph or scan every one"); (f) daily batch of 10-30 lots - the whole NFR sizing basis (V1 11,500 lots/yr, V4 peak 80/day, V5 "98% single-test (Limited Test) mix", V7 20 readings), WF-22 ("Register 30 lots for the Limited Test and assign them in a single action, in under five minutes"), and acceptance criteria AC-01/AC-02/AC-03, which are already almost verbatim the reviewer's proposed worked example ("An intake of 30 lots of the same test ... 30 sample numbers ... under 12 minutes"). Section 1's "A day in the life" narrates the same path end to end.

The fix is also not correct as drafted, and would create new contradictions. "24 samples registered in one bulk grid with one batch photograph" contradicts the M3 registration field table, where "Photograph on receipt" is Mandatory=Yes, "At least one image", per sample, and contradicts M4's per-sample receipt condition recording and weighing. A single grid spanning 9 different customers contradicts M3-15 (many samples "of the same type and test set", per request) and the per-request contract, acknowledgement slip, terms, promised date and capability-check record that M3 attaches to each Test Request. "One bulk verification batch" of 24 contradicts M7-36(c) (automatic exclusion of any allocation with a warning or plausibility confirmation) and M7-36(d) (batch size capped by configuration). The seed-data half is largely duplicative: M1 rule 1 already requires the complete Test Catalogue with prices and an Active verified Method revision per test before go-live, OPEN-Q-T18 already directs loading the 01.12.2023 rate card as it stands (which is where the 50-rupee Limited test line lives), and OPEN-Q12/OPEN-Q14 already flag Limited-test specifics as unconfirmed. Asserting one flat method with "required reading count 20" also sits awkwardly against modelling the composite through M1-32 (test bundle) / M1-33 (prerequisite tests), which is how the document handles composites.

Residual merit is at most a cosmetic cross-reference from the M3 worked example to M3-15 / M6-40 / M6-41 / M7-36 - trivial, not a Major missing capability.

rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Five different mechanisms in this section are called a repeat or a retest and none of them is defined as a record. M7-08 increments a "retest counter" on a send-back (which is rework, not a retest); M6-23 says the system "requires a repeat" when a method's repeat rule fires; M6 rules item 4 speaks of "creating the repeat set"; M10-20 "creates the repeat"; M7-38 "creates a replacement allocation linked as a repeat"; M4-13 refuses a "retest request" against exhausted material; and M5's blinding table depends on a "this is a repeat" flag that nothing sets. Unanswered for every one of them: is a repeat a new allocation on the same sample or a new sample; does it need fresh material and how does that interact with M4-13; which run does the report issue from; is the customer billed; does the due date restart; and who sets the blinding flag. A solo developer will invent five inconsistent behaviours, and the counter will not be able to answer a customer asking whether a re-test costs money.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (parts/section_3_functional_core.md:1098; SPEC.md:2343), but the finding's central claim — "none of them is defined as a record" — is factually wrong. The reviewer read only Section 3 (M4/M6/M7/M10) and missed that a repeat is defined as a record in three other places.

DEFINED AS A RECORD:
1. Data dictionary, parts/section_5_nfr_plan.md:482 (SPEC.md:5198): txn_sample_test carries `retest_count SMALLINT`, `retest_of_id`, `superseded_by_id`, `validity VARCHAR(15)`, with unique key `sample_id, test_id, retest_count`. `retest_of_id` IS the `repeat_of` pointer the fix proposes to invent, and the unique key already settles "same sample or new sample" — same sample_id, new row discriminated by retest_count.
2. Allocation state table, parts/section_2_workflow.md:607 (SPEC.md:1049-1050): Discarded → "Creates a repeat allocation in Pending, linked as a retest of this one. Does **not** re-bill the customer." Invalidated → "Creates a repeat allocation."
3. Numbering table, parts/section_2_workflow.md:734 (SPEC.md:1176): "A repeat allocation takes the next free suffix, and its lineage to the original is stored."

Section 9 ("Sample and test allocation lifecycle") is the document's declared home for allocation lifecycle semantics — two coupled state machines plus 60 transition rules WF-31..WF-90. Repeats belong there, not in M6 (result entry), so the "fragmentation" is by design.

EVERY "UNANSWERED" QUESTION IS ANSWERED:
- New allocation vs new sample: WF-86 "creates a **new** allocation linked to the original as a retest"; SPEC.md:1069; plus the DB unique key.
- Fresh material / M4-13 interaction: M4-13 itself is the answer; SPEC.md:1069 "on retained material if available"; SPEC.md:1077; Sample state In Retention → "In Testing (retest on retained material)"; acceptance case AC-15 (SPEC.md:5565).
- Which run the report issues from: WF-74 "prevents the certificate being issued from the discarded run"; SPEC.md:1071 "certificate issued from the repeat run only"; M6 rules item 4 "issuing the certificate from the repeat".
- Billing: Discarded "Does **not** re-bill the customer"; WF-86 "separately priced" + separate invoice line; WF-84 chargeability decision with a lab-at-fault list; M18-15 "The laboratory decides whether the repeat is chargeable"; OPEN-Q-B8 (SPEC.md:1145) carries the seeded policy default. A counter CAN answer whether a retest costs money.
- Due date: M7-08 / WF-77 / AC-13 all state the send-back clock keeps running and the due date is unchanged; a repeat allocation is created in Pending, whose entry action "Computes the due date, including any conditioning hours."
- Blinding flag: it exists (SPEC.md:2019) and the reviewer MISREADS it. It is a sample-family flag about repeat SAMPLES (SPEC.md:2033 "A repeat sample must be linked"; SPEC.md:2076 "Do not let the sample family identifier leak the customer"), whereas a repeat per the spec is a new allocation on the SAME sample.

The "retest counter" naming point is the only residue, and it is cosmetic: the term is used consistently in five places (M7-08, WF-77, WF-90, SPEC.md:1070, AC-13) and WF-90 pins its semantics exactly ("allocations verified with a retest count of zero" = first-time-right). It never counts repeat allocations, so there is no collision. Renaming would also require changing the DB column `retest_count`.

THE PROPOSED FIX IS ITSELF DEFECTIVE AND WOULD CREATE NEW CONTRADICTIONS:
(a) It cites "M6-51" for the conditioned-size 7% rule. M6-51 does not exist — M6 ends at M6-50. The rule is WF-74 / M6 rules item 4.
(b) "all others non-billable" contradicts WF-84 ("chargeable where the customer's material was at fault, per configuration") and OPEN-Q-B8's default that material-related causes are chargeable at a handling fee.
(c) "The report or certificate is always issued from the latest non-discarded run" directly contradicts WF-86 and SPEC.md:1069, which require that a customer-requested retest after issue "does not alter the original allocation or its report" — under the fix the retest would become the latest non-discarded run and retroactively govern report issuance.
(d) "Creating a repeat sets the 'related sample exists' flag" wires an allocation-level event to a sample-family flag, which is the wrong flag per (b) above.

The finding is a misreading driven by reading one section in isolation, and the fix would damage a part of the document that is currently correct.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: M8-27 to M8-36 (lines 1211–1220), M1-73 (line 178), OPEN-Q6 (line 1222), OPEN-Q7 (line 1224)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: Two problems, both costing a solo developer weeks for no day-one benefit. First, the whole accreditation apparatus is unreachable at go-live: the research shows certificate TC-14590 names only TTL Bengaluru, and OPEN-Q6's own recommended default configures this unit as not accredited — under which no parameter is ever in scope, so the Unique Laboratory Report number, its configuration-driven template engine (M1-73), the scope master, the automatic two-report split (M8-32), the symbol-validity asset (M8-35) and the second verification code position (OPEN-Q7) are all dead code.
