rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quoted text exists verbatim, but four of the five sub-claims are refuted by context, and the proposed fix is largely a no-op or actively harmful.

(a) MISREADING. The reviewer quotes OPEN-Q-T28 as telling us to "assume single-unit deployment" — but the *same cell* (section_5_nfr_plan.md:956) reads: "Build the multi-unit columns and scoping now; assume single-unit deployment; re-review architecture if roll-out is proposed." The document explicitly and deliberately decided the scoping layer is in, and V21 (:29) sizes a real 16-unit roll-out. The finding cuts the decision in half and quotes the half it likes. Further: AC-47 is not Phase 1 scope. The Phase 1 requirement list (:643) enumerates NFR/ARC/DB identifiers only — no AC identifiers — and Phase 6 (§26.8, :702) already includes "second-unit readiness testing", which is exactly where the fix proposes putting it. AC-47 is also not a "penetration test"; it is one negative acceptance scenario (configure a second unit's user, supply a Dharmavaram identifier, confirm refusal). And the "weeks of work" for a session-scoped query layer ignores NFR-58 (:139), already [MUST] in Phase 1, which requires access to customer identity and commercial data to be "enforced at the data layer, not by hiding fields in the screen", verified by AC-07 on the raw network response. The unit scope rides on data-layer scoping infrastructure Phase 1 must build anyway for NABL cl. 4.2 confidentiality.

(b) FACTUALLY WRONG on its central premise. The reviewer says row-level access logging is "an obligation that is not traceable to the research pack". It is directly traceable: research_india_commercial.md:680 marks the 72-hour affected-persons notification **[VERIFIED]**, and :681 is the build item — "the ability to answer '**which** data principals were affected?' in minutes rather than weeks. That requires access logs at row level for personal data, not just application logs. This is the single most under-built breach requirement." It is independently restated as M21-75 (section_4_functional_support.md:1672): "That requires access logging at record level for personal data, not only application-level logs." Also, NFR-65 is not Phase 1 scope — the Phase 1 list jumps NFR-45–58 straight to NFR-68–72, omitting the whole NFR-59–67 data-protection block.

(c) REAL, but a different defect than claimed. NFR-24 measures internal availability "by an uptime check every 5 minutes" per ARC-33, which "runs from outside the laboratory ... against both the internal system (through whatever route exists)", while NFR-27 requires all screens fully usable with the internet unplugged for 5 continuous working days, and ARC-18 (:360) states the internet-facing component has "no network route back into the laboratory network". So the stated measurement is both self-contradictory and architecturally unimplementable as written, and no exclusion clause for line outages exists anywhere (I searched availability/uptime/excluded/heartbeat across all parts). This is a measurability and internal-consistency defect in one table cell, not over-engineering — the 99.0% target itself is modest, not gold-plating.

(d) MISDESCRIBED. NFR-99 is a restore "onto the staging environment", not "onto a second machine at the unit". ARC-25 (:374) notes the restore is exercised as a by-product of normal work because every release is installed on staging anyway. research_india_commercial.md:836 recommends "an automated monthly restore test" ("An untested backup is not a backup. Government offices are full of them"), and M21-49 (section_4:1510) already makes the interval configurable with monthly as the *default*. The "lab with no IT support" premise contradicts OPEN-Q-T26's answer: a written support arrangement plus two trained administrators in the unit (PLN-26).

(e) MOSTLY FALSE. The prepared-solution register and supplier evaluation are already in Phase 3 (§26.5, :678), and the environment log is Phase 3 per the phase summary (:608) — exactly where fix item (5) proposes moving them, so that part of the fix is a no-op. mst_test_profile appears only in the full schema table (:447); it is absent from Phase 1's Included list, which names "test, method, parameter, unit-of-measure, specification and grade masters". Only scan stations are genuinely Phase 1, and the 8-station set is a direct research-pack recommendation (research_lims_reference.md §10 item 6 and §6.5) implemented over a single keyboard-wedge USB scanner mechanism (NFR-78, :182) — the marginal cost of 8 station routes over 2 is a config table, not weeks.

FIX WOULD INTRODUCE NEW CONTRADICTIONS: item (2) deletes a [VERIFIED] statutory build item and puts section_5 in direct conflict with M21-75 in section_4; item (1) reverses the recorded OPEN-Q-T28 decision without amending it; item (4) conflicts with M21-49's "default monthly" and research_india_commercial.md:836; item (5)'s two-station cut contradicts M4-24 (section_3_functional_core.md:617), which enumerates eight stations as a [MUST] minimum.

Net: the finding as filed does not stand. One narrow, salvageable defect remains inside sub-claim (c), which is a separate correctness issue of Minor severity, not the Major over-engineering thesis advanced here.

rejectedForTheRecord.location: Part E — §26.6 Phase 4 "Included" list, line 5395 (against §26.3 Phase 1 "the grading engine", line 5357)
rejectedForTheRecord.problem: The gap analysis rates the conformity statement with a decision rule (#14) and measurement uncertainty (#15) as Critical, warning "If you write 'PASS' without a recorded decision rule, it's a nonconformity — and in silk trade the pass/fail *is* the deliverable". Phase 1 includes the grading engine and the specification and grade masters, and `txn_sample_test` (a Phase 1 table) already carries `spec_set_id`, `decision_rule_id` and `overall_verdict`. Nothing in Phase 1 prevents a certificate from printing a verdict against the customer's declared 20/22 D or a specification set while `decision_rule_id` is null and no uncertainty is stored, because the Decision Rule master (M7-16), the deterministic verdict computation (M7-18) and the automatic uncertainty trigger (M7-21) all arrive in Phase 4.
rejectedForTheRecord.whyRejected:
The quote is genuine (SPEC.md:5395, Phase 4 "Included"), but the claimed gap is already closed by unconditional requirements that the reviewer treated as phase-scoped, and the proposed fix collides with an existing requirement and contradicts another.

1. The gate the reviewer asks for already exists, three times over.
- M7-15 (SPEC.md:2295) [MUST]: "A conformity statement (a pass or fail against a specification) may be made only where the customer requested one, the specification was recorded at request time, and a decision rule was selected and agreed with the customer at request time. None of these may be chosen at verification time." Before the Decision Rule master is live this precondition is unsatisfiable, so M7-15 self-enforces exactly the Phase-1 fallback the reviewer wants to legislate.
- M7-20 (SPEC.md:2310) [MUST]: "Where no conformity statement was requested, the report presents results with no pass or fail wording anywhere. The system must not volunteer a verdict." Acceptance check: "no pass, fail, satisfactory or unsatisfactory wording appears."
- M8-18 (SPEC.md:2441) [MUST]: where a conformity statement is made the report must name "the decision rule applied"; enforced at issue by M8-42 (SPEC.md:2486), whose atomic "mandatory content check" is in Phase 1 and issues nothing if any step fails. M8-19 (SPEC.md:2442) does the same for uncertainty "whenever it affects conformity against a limit."

2. The reviewer conflates feature delivery with requirement applicability. Phase 1's identifier list (SPEC.md:5358) enumerates only NFR, ARC and DB ranges — M-requirements are never assigned to phases anywhere in §26. M7-15 and M7-20 are prohibitions, not features; nothing needs building for them to bind. The "Included:" prose says what gets coded, not which MUSTs are suspended.

3. The Phase-1 gate is also in Phase 1 explicitly. "Verification with send-back" is in the Phase 1 Included list, and M7-11/M7-12 (SPEC.md:2288) make the verification checklist blocking, with item (o) "where a conformity statement is to be made, the specification, the decision rule and the computed verdict are consistent" and item (p) "where measurement uncertainty must be reported, it is present and in the correct unit." Any No blocks verification.

4. The Phase-1 capability the reviewer points at is precisely the case the document says needs no decision rule or uncertainty. Phase 1 ships "the grading engine" = WF-73 (SPEC.md:1124), which reads results against "the dated, category-specific classification tables of the selected specification set" and outputs a grade letter. M7-19's fourth named rule, "Prescribed by the specification," states: "Where the standard is silent on uncertainty (as the raw-silk grading tables are), the classification tables are applied to the measured value as written," and M7-23 separates "a parameter's grade or class is assigned rather than a numeric verdict." Phase 1's own outcome text says "have the average, deviation and grade computed" — grade, not verdict. Phase 1's Included list never mentions conformity.

5. The scenario is not reachable in Phase 1 anyway. The only place a spec set and decision rule can be captured is txn_order (the Test Request Form: decision_rule_id, decision_rule_agreed_on, spec_set_id, SPEC.md:5193), and the TRF with recorded request review is Phase 2 (§26.4). The research brief agrees — research_gap_analysis.md:338 calls the TRF "the only place declared denier, spec limits and decision rule can be captured." So in Phase 1 there is no request record to carry a conformity request, and any printed verdict would be the system volunteering one, which M7-20 forbids outright.

6. The proposed fix is defective on its own terms. M8-64 is already taken — it is the duplicate-copy requirement (SPEC.md:2518, "DUPLICATE COPY" overlay and counter), and M8 runs through M8-68. And the wording contradicts M8-18: it would require "a stored decision rule reference" for the words "meets, satisfies, within specification," whereas M8-18 deliberately exempts the case where the rule "is inherent in the cited specification" — the raw-silk grading tables. A Grading Certificate stating a lot meets the 2A classification would be refused by the reviewer's rule and required by M8-18.

The only residual is cosmetic: §26.3 could name M7-15 and M7-20 in Phase 1 for the avoidance of doubt. That is editorial cross-referencing, not a compliance risk, and does not support a Major finding.
